ENT-01.Sole proprietorship: A business owned and run by one person, who keeps all the profit and is personally responsible for all its debts.
ENT-01.Corporation: A business that is a legal entity separate from its owners, the shareholders. They are not personally liable for its debts, but a regular corporation's profit can be taxed twice.
ENT-01.Partnership: A business owned by two or more people who share the profits, the work and, in a general partnership, personal responsibility for the debts.
ENT-01.LLC: A limited liability company protects its owners' personal assets like a corporation does, while its profit is usually taxed only once, on the owners' own tax returns.
ENT-01.Franchise: A business run under a license from a larger company, the franchisor. The owner pays fees to use its name, products and operating system.
ENT-01.Nonprofit: An organization set up to serve a cause instead of earning profit for owners. Any surplus goes back into its mission, and it can qualify for tax-exempt status.
ENT-01.S corporation: A corporation that chooses a special tax status so its profit passes through to shareholders' personal returns, avoiding double taxation. The number of shareholders is limited.
ENT-01.Cooperative: A business owned and controlled by the members who use it, such as farmers or shoppers. Members usually get one vote each and share in any surplus.
ENT-01.Limited partnership: A partnership with at least one general partner who runs the business and is fully liable, plus limited partners who only invest and risk only what they put in. A limited liability partnership (LLP) instead shields every partner.
ENT-01.Joint venture: An agreement between two or more businesses to work together on one specific project, sharing its costs, risks and profits, often for a limited time.
ENT-01.B corporation: A for-profit company committed to social and environmental goals as well as profit, either by outside certification (Certified B Corp) or by its legal form (benefit corporation).
ENT-01.Professional corporation: A corporation formed by licensed professionals such as doctors, lawyers or accountants. Each stays personally liable for their own malpractice.
ENT-01.Close corporation: A corporation owned by a small group of people, often family, whose shares are not sold to the public. It can run with fewer formalities than a large corporation.

ENT-02.Bank loan: Money borrowed from a bank or credit union and repaid with interest over a set time. The founder keeps full ownership but must make the payments.
ENT-02.Personal savings: The founder's own money put into the business. It is the most common starting source and needs no repayment or sharing of ownership.
ENT-02.Venture capital: Money from professional investment firms that buy a share of young companies with high growth potential, hoping to profit when the company is sold or goes public.
ENT-02.Crowdfunding: Raising small amounts of money from many people, usually through a website, in return for rewards, early products or sometimes shares.
ENT-02.Angel investor: A wealthy individual who invests their own money in a very young business, usually in exchange for part ownership, and often gives advice too.
ENT-02.Friends and family: Loans, gifts or investments from people the founder knows personally. The terms are often easy, but personal relationships are put at risk.
ENT-02.Bootstrapping: Building the business with the founder's own money and the cash the business earns, instead of outside loans or investors.
ENT-02.Business partner: Someone who joins the business as a co-owner and contributes money, skills or both in return for a share of ownership and profit.
ENT-02.Grants: Money given by a government agency, foundation or company for a stated purpose. A grant does not have to be repaid, but it is competitive and comes with conditions.
ENT-02.SBA loan: A loan made by a bank and partly guaranteed by the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA), which makes lenders more willing to lend to small firms.
ENT-02.Credit cards: Borrowing by charging business purchases to a personal or business card. It is quick to get but carries high interest if the balance is not paid off.
ENT-02.Line of credit: An arrangement with a lender to borrow up to a set limit whenever cash is needed. Interest is paid only on the amount actually borrowed.
ENT-02.Selling personal assets: Raising startup cash by selling things the founder owns, such as a car, jewelry or investments.
ENT-02.Accelerator: A short, intensive program that gives selected startups mentoring, contacts and often a small investment, usually for a share of ownership. Incubators offer similar early support.
ENT-02.Initial public offering: The first sale of a company's shares to the general public on a stock exchange. It raises large sums but is realistic only for established, growing companies.
ENT-02.Microloan: A very small loan, often a few hundred to tens of thousands of dollars, made by nonprofit or community lenders to owners who may not qualify for a bank loan.
ENT-02.Home equity loan: A loan secured by the owner's house, based on the part of its value that is already paid for. If it is not repaid, the home can be lost.
ENT-02.Trade credit: Buying supplies or inventory from a supplier now and paying later, often in 30 days. It works as a short, usually interest-free loan.
ENT-02.Pitch competition: A contest in which founders present their business ideas to judges, with prize money or investment for the winners.
ENT-02.Pre-sales: Taking orders and payment from customers before the product is made, so customers' money helps pay for production.
ENT-02.Peer-to-peer lending: Borrowing through an online platform that matches borrowers directly with individuals or investors willing to lend, without a traditional bank in the middle.
ENT-02.Equipment leasing: Paying a regular fee to use equipment instead of buying it outright, which lowers the cash needed at the start.
ENT-02.Convertible note: A short-term loan from an investor that is meant to turn into shares of the company later, usually at the next funding round, instead of being repaid in cash.
ENT-02.Revenue-based financing: Money from investors that is repaid as a fixed percentage of the company's monthly sales until an agreed total has been paid. No ownership is given up.
ENT-02.Retirement funds: Using money saved in a retirement account such as a 401(k) or IRA to start the business. It risks the founder's retirement and strict tax rules apply.
ENT-02.Corporate venture capital: Investment in a startup by a large company instead of an investment firm, often because the startup's product or technology fits the big company's strategy.

ENT-03.Executive summary: A short overview at the front of the plan that sums up the business, its market, its goals and the money it needs. Many readers decide from it whether to read on.
ENT-03.Financial plan: The numbers section: projected income, costs, cash flow and break-even point, showing whether the business can make money and repay lenders.
ENT-03.Marketing plan: Explains how the business will reach and win customers, covering product, price, place (distribution) and promotion.
ENT-03.Company description: Describes what the business is and does, including its history, the need it meets and what makes it different.
ENT-03.Market analysis: Research on the industry, the target customers and the size and trends of the market, showing there is real demand.
ENT-03.Products and services: Describes exactly what the business will sell, its features and benefits, and how it compares with what is already available.
ENT-03.Operations plan: Explains how the business will run day to day: how the product is made or delivered, the suppliers, the equipment and the processes used.
ENT-03.Management team: Introduces the people who will run the business, their experience and roles, and how the organization is structured.
ENT-03.Competitive analysis: Identifies the main competitors, their strengths and weaknesses, and how the new business will stand out against them.
ENT-03.Mission statement: A brief statement of the purpose of the business: what it does, for whom and why. A vision statement adds where it hopes to be in the future.
ENT-03.Goals and objectives: The specific results the business aims to reach, such as sales targets or opening dates, usually with deadlines so progress can be measured.
ENT-03.SWOT analysis: A review of the internal Strengths and Weaknesses of the business and the external Opportunities and Threats it faces.
ENT-03.Funding request: States how much money the business needs, what type (loan or investment), what it will be used for and how lenders will be repaid or investors rewarded.
ENT-03.Risk analysis: Lists the main things that could go wrong, such as new competitors or rising costs, and explains how the business would deal with them.
ENT-03.Legal structure: States the form of ownership chosen, such as sole proprietorship, partnership, LLC or corporation, and who owns what share.
ENT-03.Cover page: The first page of the plan, showing the business name, logo, the owners' names, contact details and the date.
ENT-03.Table of contents: A list of the plan's sections with page numbers, so a lender or investor can find any part quickly.
ENT-03.Location and facilities: Describes where the business will operate, the building and space it needs, and why that site suits its customers or operations.
ENT-03.Appendix: The back section that holds supporting documents such as resumes, permits, leases, market research data and detailed financial tables.
ENT-03.Exit strategy: Explains how the owners or investors plan to eventually leave the business and get their money out, for example by selling it or passing it on.
ENT-03.Milestones: A timeline of key steps and target dates, such as finishing a prototype, opening the doors or reaching break-even.
ENT-03.Staffing plan: Sets out which jobs the business needs to fill, when it will hire, and what the employees will cost.

ENT-04.Risk-taking: Willingness to put time and money into something that might fail. Successful entrepreneurs take calculated risks, weighing the odds first instead of gambling.
ENT-04.Creativity: The ability to come up with new ideas or new ways of doing things, which is how entrepreneurs find products and solutions others have missed.
ENT-04.Persistence: Continuing to work toward a goal despite setbacks and failures. Most new businesses hit obstacles, so owners who give up early rarely succeed.
ENT-04.Self-confidence: Belief in your own abilities and ideas. It helps an entrepreneur make decisions, sell the idea to others and keep going when people doubt it.
ENT-04.Passion: Strong enthusiasm for the business or the problem it solves, which supplies the energy to work long hours and inspires customers and staff.
ENT-04.Hard-working: Willing to put in long hours and steady effort. A new owner often does many jobs at once, especially in the first years.
ENT-04.Self-motivation: The inner drive to get started and keep working without a boss giving orders or setting deadlines.
ENT-04.Independence: A wish to make your own decisions and rely on yourself instead of being directed by others. It is a common reason people start businesses.
ENT-04.Goal-oriented: Focused on setting clear targets and working steadily to reach them. Entrepreneurs often have a strong need to achieve.
ENT-04.Leadership: The ability to guide and inspire other people, such as employees, partners and investors, to work toward the goals of the business.
ENT-04.Adaptability: The ability to change plans quickly when customers, competitors or conditions change, instead of sticking to an idea that is no longer working.
ENT-04.Vision: A clear picture of what the business could become in the future, which guides decisions and helps persuade others to join in.
ENT-04.Problem solving: The skill of working out what is going wrong and finding a practical fix, often with limited money and time.
ENT-04.Integrity: Being honest and keeping your word. Customers, suppliers, lenders and employees deal more readily with an owner they can trust.
ENT-04.Optimism: Expecting things to work out and seeing setbacks as temporary, which helps an entrepreneur keep trying after a disappointment.
ENT-04.Communication skills: The ability to explain ideas clearly, listen well and persuade. Entrepreneurs use it to sell, negotiate, lead staff and win over investors.
ENT-04.Responsibility: Accepting that the results of the business, good or bad, are your own doing, and following through on what you promise.
ENT-04.Self-discipline: The ability to make yourself do what needs doing, even when it is dull or difficult, and to manage your own time and money carefully.
ENT-04.Action-oriented: Inclined to act on ideas and take the first step without waiting to be told. Ideas only become businesses when someone acts on them.
ENT-04.Organized: Able to plan, set priorities and keep track of time, money and tasks, which matters when one person is handling many parts of a business.
ENT-04.Competitiveness: A strong desire to do better than rivals, which pushes an entrepreneur to keep improving the product and the service.
ENT-04.Opportunity recognition: The ability to notice an unmet need or a gap in the market and see how a business could fill it.
ENT-04.Energetic: Having the physical and mental stamina to handle the long days and heavy workload of starting and running a business.
ENT-04.Decisiveness: The ability to make a choice promptly with the information available. Owners must often decide quickly and cannot wait for certainty.
ENT-04.Willingness to learn: Openness to new knowledge, advice and feedback, including learning from your own mistakes and failures.
ENT-04.Curiosity: A habit of asking questions and wondering why things are done a certain way, which is often how new business opportunities get noticed.
ENT-04.Patience: Being able to wait for results. Most businesses take months or years to become profitable, so owners must stay steady in the meantime.
ENT-04.Internal locus of control: The belief that your own choices and effort, not luck or other people, decide what happens to you. Research often finds it in entrepreneurs.
ENT-04.Tolerance for ambiguity: Being comfortable acting when the situation is unclear and the outcome uncertain, which is normal when starting something new.

ENT-05.Small business entrepreneurship: Starting and running a small, usually local firm such as a shop, salon or restaurant, aiming to earn a living for the owner instead of growing into a giant.
ENT-05.Social entrepreneurship: Starting an organization mainly to solve a social or environmental problem, using business methods. Success is measured by impact as well as money.
ENT-05.Scalable startup: A new company built from the start to grow very large and fast, often using technology and outside investors' money.
ENT-05.Serial entrepreneur: A person who starts one business after another, often selling or handing over each one before moving to the next idea.
ENT-05.Online entrepreneurship: Building a business that sells or operates mainly over the internet, such as an online store, app or digital service.
ENT-05.Franchisee: A person who buys the right to open and run an outlet of an established brand, following the franchisor's system and paying fees.
ENT-05.Intrapreneurship: Acting like an entrepreneur inside an existing company: an employee develops a new product or venture using the employer's resources.
ENT-05.Lifestyle entrepreneur: Someone who builds a business around a personal passion or preferred way of living, valuing freedom and enjoyment above fast growth.
ENT-05.Solopreneur: A person who runs a business entirely alone, with no employees or partners, such as a freelancer or independent consultant.
ENT-05.Family business: A business owned and run by members of one family, often passed down from one generation to the next.
ENT-05.Home-based business: A business operated from the owner's home instead of a separate shop or office, which keeps costs low.
ENT-05.Innovative entrepreneur: An entrepreneur who introduces something truly new, such as a new product, production method or market. It is one of four types named by Clarence Danhof.
ENT-05.Green entrepreneurship: Starting a business whose products or operations are designed to protect the environment, such as recycling or clean energy. Its founders are also called ecopreneurs.
ENT-05.Technopreneur: An entrepreneur whose business is built on technology, for example software, apps or electronic devices.
ENT-05.Part-time entrepreneur: Someone who runs a business on the side while keeping another job or studying, often called a side hustle.
ENT-05.Hustler entrepreneur: An informal label for a founder who starts small and relies on hard work and persistent selling, not large capital, to grow the business step by step.
ENT-05.Agripreneur: An entrepreneur in agriculture, who starts a business in farming, food production or related services.
ENT-05.Imitative entrepreneur: An entrepreneur who copies or adapts an idea that has already succeeded elsewhere instead of inventing a new one. One of Danhof's four types.
ENT-05.Buyer entrepreneur: A person who becomes a business owner by buying an existing business, then running and improving it, instead of starting from nothing.
ENT-05.Necessity entrepreneur: Someone who starts a business because they have no better way to earn a living, for example after losing a job.
ENT-05.Opportunity entrepreneur: Someone who starts a business by choice because they have spotted a promising opportunity, not because they lack other work.
ENT-05.Fabian entrepreneur: A very cautious entrepreneur who adopts a new idea only when it is clear that not changing would hurt the business. One of Danhof's four types.
ENT-05.Drone entrepreneur: An entrepreneur who refuses to change methods or products even when the business is losing ground to others. One of Danhof's four types.
ENT-05.Researcher entrepreneur: An informal label for a founder who gathers and analyzes a great deal of information before acting, relying on facts and careful planning over instinct.

ENT-06.Hobbies and interests: Things you already enjoy and know well, such as baking, gaming or sports. Your knowledge of the activity helps you see what its fans would pay for.
ENT-06.Everyday problems: Annoyances and unmet needs that you or other people run into. A product or service that removes the problem is the classic business idea.
ENT-06.Work experience: Knowledge gained in past or current jobs. Employees often notice what their industry does badly and start a business that does it better.
ENT-06.Trends: Changes in what people buy, do or care about, such as healthier eating. Spotting a trend early lets a business meet new demand first.
ENT-06.Existing products: Goods and services already on sale. Improving one, or fixing a weakness in what competitors offer, is a common source of ideas.
ENT-06.New technology: Inventions and scientific advances that make new products possible or old ones cheaper, opening room for new businesses.
ENT-06.Market research: Gathering information from customers through surveys, feedback and other studies to learn what they want and are not getting.
ENT-06.Friends and family: People you know, whose comments, complaints and suggestions in ordinary conversation can point to a need a business could meet.
ENT-06.Internet and social media: Websites, forums and social platforms where you can see what people are talking about, searching for and complaining about.
ENT-06.Brainstorming: A creative session in which a person or group lists as many ideas as possible without judging them, then sorts out the best afterwards.
ENT-06.Travel: Visiting other cities or countries, where you may see products or services that work well there but are not yet offered at home.
ENT-06.Trade shows: Events where the businesses in an industry display their newest products, letting visitors see what is coming and what is missing.
ENT-06.Education: Classes, courses and training, which give knowledge and skills that can suggest a business, and often include projects that spark ideas.
ENT-06.Observation: Simply watching how people live, shop and work, and noticing where they struggle or make do with something that could be better.
ENT-06.Trade publications: Magazines, journals and news written for a particular industry, which report new developments, trends and gaps in that field.
ENT-06.Demographic changes: Shifts in the make-up of the population, such as more elderly people or more single households, that create new groups of customers with new needs.
ENT-06.Franchise opportunities: Ready-made business concepts offered by franchisors. Someone looking for an idea can buy the right to open a tested business instead of inventing one.
ENT-06.Suppliers and distributors: Businesses that make and move products through the channel. They know the market closely and often pass on what customers are asking for.
ENT-06.Focus groups: Small groups of potential customers brought together to discuss a product area with a moderator, revealing wants and complaints.
ENT-06.Economic changes: Shifts such as rising incomes, recession or inflation that change what people can afford and need, creating demand for different products.
ENT-06.Changes in laws: New rules or the removal of old ones. A new safety or environmental law, for example, can create demand for products that help people comply.
ENT-06.Government sources: Public agencies and their records, including patent filings and published statistics, which can reveal inventions and market needs.
ENT-06.University research: Discoveries made in university and research laboratories, which can be licensed or developed into commercial products.
ENT-06.Unexpected events: Surprises, such as an unplanned success, a failure or an accident, that reveal a need nobody had seen. Peter Drucker listed the unexpected as a source of innovation.
ENT-06.Industry changes: Shifts in how an industry is organized, such as rapid growth or new ways of selling, that leave openings for newcomers. Another of Drucker's sources of innovation.

ENT-07.Being your own boss: The owner makes the decisions and answers to no manager. Independence is the reason many entrepreneurs give first for starting a business.
ENT-07.Profit potential: The chance to earn more than a wage. The owner keeps what the business makes, so there is no fixed ceiling on income, though there is no guarantee either.
ENT-07.Flexible schedule: The freedom to decide when and where to work. Owners often work long hours, but they choose which hours those are.
ENT-07.Personal satisfaction: The pride and sense of achievement that come from building something of your own and seeing it succeed.
ENT-07.Creative freedom: The chance to try your own ideas and build the business the way you imagine it, without needing someone else's approval.
ENT-07.Doing what you love: The opportunity to earn a living from an activity or subject you care about, so that work is enjoyable.
ENT-07.Recognition: The respect and standing a successful business owner can earn in the community and the industry.
ENT-07.Helping the community: The good a business does for others: it creates jobs, serves local needs, pays taxes and can support local causes.
ENT-07.Leadership opportunity: The chance to lead a team and shape how an organization works, instead of following someone else's direction.
ENT-07.Challenge: The excitement and variety of the work. Every day brings new problems to solve, which many entrepreneurs find more rewarding than routine.
ENT-07.Personal growth: The skills and experience gained by running a business, from selling and managing money to leading people.
ENT-07.Job security: An owner cannot be fired or laid off by an employer. The job lasts as long as the business survives, which depends on the owner's own efforts.
ENT-07.Choosing who you work with: The owner decides whom to hire and which partners, suppliers and customers to deal with.
ENT-07.Tax deductions: Legitimate business costs, such as equipment, travel for work or a home office, can be subtracted from business income before tax is worked out.
ENT-07.Building equity: As the business grows in value, the owner's share of it becomes an asset that can one day be sold or borrowed against.
ENT-07.Family legacy: A successful business can be handed on to children or other relatives, giving them work, income and something lasting.

SUP-01.Customer segments: The different groups of people or organizations the business aims to reach and serve.
SUP-01.Value propositions: The bundle of products and services that creates value for a customer segment: the reason customers choose this business over another.
SUP-01.Revenue streams: The ways the business earns money from each customer segment, such as sales, subscriptions or fees.
SUP-01.Channels: How the business reaches its customers to communicate with them, sell to them and deliver the product, such as stores, a website or a sales team.
SUP-01.Customer relationships: The kind of relationship the business sets up with each customer segment, from personal service to self-service or automated help.
SUP-01.Cost structure: All the main costs of operating the business model, such as wages, materials, rent and marketing.
SUP-01.Key activities: The most important things the business must do to make its model work, such as production, problem solving or running a platform.
SUP-01.Key resources: The most important assets the model needs, which may be physical, financial, intellectual (such as patents and brands) or human.
SUP-01.Key partnerships: The network of suppliers and partners the business relies on, for example to obtain resources or carry out some activities.

SUP-02.Equipment: The machines, tools and vehicles the business needs before it can operate, such as ovens for a bakery or a van for deliveries.
SUP-02.Inventory: The first stock of goods to sell, or the raw materials to make them, which must be bought before any sales are made.
SUP-02.Rent or building: The cost of a place to operate: a security deposit and first rent on leased space, or the down payment to buy a building or land.
SUP-02.Licenses and permits: Fees paid to government bodies for legal permission to operate, such as a business license or a health permit.
SUP-02.Marketing: The cost of telling customers the business exists before it opens, including a logo, business cards, signs and opening advertisements.
SUP-02.Payroll: Wages for employees hired before opening, plus the cost of recruiting them. Staff must be paid even before sales begin.
SUP-02.Insurance: Premiums paid up front for policies that protect the new business against losses such as fire, theft or injury claims.
SUP-02.Legal fees: Payments to lawyers and accountants for setting up the business properly, such as drafting contracts and setting up the books.
SUP-02.Website and technology: Computers, software, a website and a checkout or point-of-sale system needed to take orders and run the business.
SUP-02.Supplies: Items used up in running the business and not sold to customers, such as paper, cleaning products and packaging, bought before opening.
SUP-02.Furniture and fixtures: Desks, chairs, shelving, counters and display cases that fit out the space for staff and customers.
SUP-02.Renovations: Building work to make a space suitable, such as new walls, flooring, plumbing or paint. Changes to a rented space are called leasehold improvements.
SUP-02.Utility deposits: Deposits and connection charges paid to electricity, water, gas and internet providers before service starts.
SUP-02.Franchise fee: A one-time payment to a franchisor for the right to open an outlet under its brand. It applies only when the new business is a franchise.
SUP-02.Signage: The signs outside and inside the premises that identify the business and guide customers.
SUP-02.Incorporation fees: Charges paid to the state to register the business legally, for example to file the papers that create a corporation or LLC.
SUP-02.Employee training: The cost of teaching new staff their jobs before opening day, including their wages while they learn.
SUP-02.Market research: Money spent studying customers, competitors and demand before launching, to check that the idea can succeed.
SUP-02.Product development: The cost of designing the product and building and testing prototypes before it is ready to sell.
SUP-02.Patents and trademarks: Government filing fees and legal costs for protecting an invention (patent) or a brand name and logo (trademark).
SUP-02.Grand opening event: A launch event to draw attention and first customers, with costs such as decorations, giveaways and special advertising.
SUP-02.Working capital reserve: Cash set aside to pay everyday bills such as rent and wages during the first months, until sales bring in enough money.
SUP-02.Uniforms: Work clothing bought for employees so that staff look consistent and are easy for customers to recognize.
SUP-02.Security system: Alarms, cameras and locks installed to protect the premises, stock and cash from theft.

SUP-03.Get a business license: Obtain the basic permission from a city, county or state to operate a business in that place.
SUP-03.Obtain permits: Get the specific approvals the type of business needs, such as a health permit for serving food or a building permit for construction.
SUP-03.Choose a legal structure: Decide the form of ownership, such as sole proprietorship, partnership, LLC or corporation. It determines liability, taxes and paperwork.
SUP-03.Register the business name: Record the name the business will trade under. Using a name other than the owner's own usually requires a DBA ("doing business as") filing.
SUP-03.Get an EIN: Apply to the Internal Revenue Service for an Employer Identification Number (EIN), the federal tax ID a business uses to file taxes and hire staff.
SUP-03.Open a business bank account: Set up an account in the name of the business so that its money is kept separate from the owner's personal money.
SUP-03.File articles of incorporation: Submit the document that creates a corporation to the state, usually the secretary of state. An LLC files articles of organization instead.
SUP-03.Register for state taxes: Sign up with the state tax agency, for example for a seller's permit that allows the business to collect sales tax from customers.
SUP-03.Get business insurance: Buy policies that cover risks such as property damage and injury claims. Some types are required by law, by landlords or by lenders.
SUP-03.Check zoning laws: Confirm that local land-use rules allow that kind of business at the chosen address before signing a lease or opening.
SUP-03.Register a trademark or patent: File with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office to protect a brand name or logo (trademark) or an invention (patent) from being used by others.
SUP-03.Write a partnership agreement: Put in writing how the partners will share profits, work and decisions. The matching document for an LLC is called an operating agreement.
SUP-03.Pass inspections: Have officials such as health, fire or building inspectors check the premises and approve it as safe before opening.
SUP-03.Get a professional license: Obtain the state license required to practice certain occupations, such as cosmetology, accounting, real estate or contracting.
SUP-03.Buy workers compensation insurance: Take out the insurance that pays medical costs and lost wages for employees hurt on the job. Most states require it once a business has employees.
SUP-03.Adopt corporate bylaws: Approve the written internal rules of a corporation, covering matters such as how directors are chosen and how meetings and votes are held.
SUP-03.Appoint a registered agent: Name a person or company with an address in the state to receive lawsuits and official notices for the business. Corporations and LLCs must have one.
SUP-03.Register for unemployment insurance tax: Sign up as an employer with the state so the business can pay the tax that funds benefits for workers who lose their jobs.

SUP-04.Market feasibility: Whether enough customers want the product: the study looks at the size of the market, the demand and the industry.
SUP-04.Financial feasibility: Whether the numbers work: the startup money needed, where it will come from, and whether the expected sales can cover costs and earn a profit.
SUP-04.Technical feasibility: Whether the product can actually be made or delivered with the technology, equipment and know-how available.
SUP-04.Competition: A look at who already serves these customers, how strong they are, and whether a newcomer can win a share of the market.
SUP-04.Product feasibility: Whether the product or service itself is appealing: do customers like the concept, and would they buy it?
SUP-04.Operational feasibility: Whether the business can be run day to day as planned, with workable processes, suppliers and staffing.
SUP-04.Legal feasibility: Whether the idea is allowed by law and can meet the licenses, regulations and other legal requirements that apply.
SUP-04.Location feasibility: Whether a suitable and affordable site exists, with the customers, access and facilities the business needs.
SUP-04.Organizational feasibility: Whether the founders and managers have the skills and experience to carry the idea out, and whether the right team can be put together.
SUP-04.Resource feasibility: Whether the people, materials, equipment and other resources the business needs can be obtained in sufficient quantity.
SUP-04.Risk assessment: Identifying what could go wrong with the idea and judging how likely and how damaging each risk would be.
SUP-04.Environmental feasibility: Whether the project would harm the natural environment and whether it can meet environmental rules.
SUP-04.Scheduling feasibility: Whether the project can be completed in the time available, for example before a deadline or before the opportunity passes.
SUP-04.Cultural feasibility: Whether the idea fits the values, customs and attitudes of the community or organization where it would operate.

SUP-05.Cost: What the site costs to rent or buy and to occupy. A prime spot costs more, so the owner must weigh the price against the extra sales it brings.
SUP-05.Customer traffic: The number of people who walk or drive past the site. More passers-by means more potential customers, which matters most for retailers and restaurants.
SUP-05.Parking: Whether customers and staff have enough convenient places to park. Shoppers may go elsewhere if parking is hard to find.
SUP-05.Visibility: How easily the business and its sign can be seen from the street. A business that people notice needs less advertising to be found.
SUP-05.Competition: How many similar businesses are nearby. Too many can split the customers, though clusters of rivals sometimes draw shoppers to an area.
SUP-05.Proximity to customers: How close the site is to the people the business wants to serve, judged by the population, incomes and other demographics of the area.
SUP-05.Accessibility: How easy the site is to reach by road, public transportation or on foot, including for deliveries and for people with disabilities.
SUP-05.Building size: Whether the space is the right size and layout for the business and is in good condition.
SUP-05.Safety: The level of crime in the area. Customers and employees avoid places where they feel unsafe, and insurance costs more there.
SUP-05.Zoning: Local rules that set which kinds of activity are allowed on each piece of land. A site must be zoned for the type of business planned.
SUP-05.Labor supply: Whether enough workers with the right skills live within reach of the site, and what wages they expect.
SUP-05.Proximity to suppliers: How close the site is to the sources of materials or stock. Being near suppliers cuts delivery time and cost, which matters most to manufacturers.
SUP-05.Neighborhood image: The reputation and look of the surrounding area, which customers link with the business itself.
SUP-05.Taxes: State and local tax rates, which differ from place to place. Some areas also offer tax breaks to attract new businesses.
SUP-05.Room to expand: Whether the site has space for the business to grow later without having to move.
SUP-05.Lease terms: The conditions of the rental contract, such as its length, rent increases, renewal rights and who pays for repairs.
SUP-05.Community growth: Whether the population and economy of the area are growing or shrinking, which shapes future sales.
SUP-05.Shipping access: How easily goods can be moved in and out, for example by nearby highways, ports, rail lines or loading docks.
SUP-05.Infrastructure: The basic services at the site, such as roads, electricity, water and fast internet, and how reliable and costly they are.
SUP-05.Complementary businesses: Nearby businesses that attract the same customers without competing, such as a gym beside a smoothie shop or a large anchor store in a mall.
SUP-05.Quality of life: How attractive the area is to live in, including housing costs, schools and leisure. It affects the owner and the ability to attract employees.
SUP-05.Climate: The local weather, which matters for businesses that depend on it, such as outdoor recreation, farming or seasonal goods.

SUP-06.Accountant: A professional who sets up the financial records, prepares financial statements and tax returns, and advises on the finances. A CPA is a certified public accountant.
SUP-06.Attorney: A lawyer, who advises on the legal structure, contracts, leases, licenses and other legal matters, and helps the owner avoid lawsuits.
SUP-06.Banker: A bank officer who can explain loans, lines of credit and business accounts, and who decides or advises on whether the bank will lend.
SUP-06.Mentor: An experienced business person who gives guidance and shares lessons from their own career, often for free through programs such as SCORE.
SUP-06.Insurance agent: A professional who identifies the risks a business faces and sells the policies that cover them, such as property and liability insurance.
SUP-06.Bookkeeper: A person who records the day-to-day financial transactions of the business, such as sales, bills and payroll, and keeps the books up to date.
SUP-06.Business consultant: An outside expert paid to analyze a business and recommend how to plan, solve problems or improve performance.
SUP-06.Financial advisor: A professional who helps the owner plan money matters, such as investing, saving for retirement and separating personal from business finances.
SUP-06.Marketing consultant: A specialist who helps a business identify its target customers and plan branding, advertising and promotion.
SUP-06.SBA counselor: An adviser connected with the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA), which offers free or low-cost guidance on planning, loans and government programs.
SUP-06.Commercial real estate agent: An agent who helps a business find, compare and negotiate the lease or purchase of a shop, office or other premises.
SUP-06.Business coach: A professional who works with the owner one to one to set goals, build skills and stay accountable for reaching them.
SUP-06.IT consultant: An information technology (IT) specialist who advises on and sets up computers, software, websites, networks and data security.
SUP-06.Human resources consultant: A specialist who advises on hiring, pay, benefits, workplace policies and employment law.
SUP-06.Advisory board: A group of experienced people who meet to give the founder advice. Unlike a board of directors, it has no legal authority over the company.
SUP-06.Patent attorney: A lawyer qualified to file patent applications and advise on protecting inventions and other intellectual property.

SUP-07.Division of profits and losses: How the partners will share what the business earns or loses. Without a written rule, state law usually splits it equally.
SUP-07.Capital contributions: What each partner puts into the business at the start, whether cash, property or equipment, and whether more may be required later.
SUP-07.Duties of each partner: Who is responsible for which parts of the work and what authority each partner has to act for the business.
SUP-07.Names of the partners: The identity of every person who is a partner, so that it is clear who is bound by the agreement.
SUP-07.Ownership percentages: The share of the business that each partner owns, which need not be equal.
SUP-07.Decision making: How choices will be made: which decisions one partner can make alone, which need a vote, and how votes are counted.
SUP-07.Withdrawal of a partner: What happens if a partner leaves, retires, becomes disabled or dies, including how that partner's share will be valued and bought out.
SUP-07.Dissolution: How the partnership can be ended and how its assets and debts will be divided when it is.
SUP-07.Business name and purpose: The name the partnership will operate under and a description of the kind of business it will carry on.
SUP-07.Dispute resolution: The method for settling disagreements between partners, such as mediation or arbitration, without going to court.
SUP-07.Salaries and draws: Whether partners are paid regularly for their work and how much cash each may take out of the business. A draw is a withdrawal against a partner's share.
SUP-07.Liability of each partner: How the partners share the debts and legal obligations of the business among themselves. In a general partnership, outside creditors can still pursue any partner personally.
SUP-07.Admission of new partners: The procedure for bringing in another partner, such as requiring every existing partner to agree.
SUP-07.Duration: How long the partnership is meant to last: for a fixed period, until a project is finished, or indefinitely.
SUP-07.Time commitment: How many hours each partner is expected to work in the business, which prevents arguments about unequal effort.
SUP-07.Accounting records: How the books will be kept, what accounting method and fiscal year will be used, and each partner's right to inspect the records.
SUP-07.Non-compete clause: A term limiting a partner's right to run or work for a competing business, during the partnership or for a time after leaving.
SUP-07.Check-signing authority: Who is allowed to sign checks, use the bank accounts and commit the business to contracts.
SUP-07.Place of business: The main address where the partnership will operate and keep its records.

SUP-08.Product sales: The simplest model: the business sells goods to customers, one purchase at a time, for more than they cost to make or buy.
SUP-08.Subscription: Customers pay a regular fee, often monthly or yearly, for continuing access to a product or service, giving the business steady recurring income.
SUP-08.Advertising: The product is free or cheap for users, and the business earns money by charging other companies to show ads to that audience.
SUP-08.Service fees: Customers pay for work done for them instead of for a physical product, charged by the hour, by the project or as a set fee.
SUP-08.Freemium: A basic version is free to everyone, and the business earns money from the smaller group of users who pay to upgrade to extra features.
SUP-08.Commission: The business brings a buyer and a seller together and keeps a percentage or fee from each sale, as marketplaces and brokers do.
SUP-08.Rental: Customers pay to use something for a limited time without owning it, such as a car, tools or equipment.
SUP-08.Franchising: The business lets others open outlets under its brand and system, and earns an upfront franchise fee plus ongoing royalties on their sales.
SUP-08.Licensing: The owner of intellectual property, such as a patent, brand or character, charges others a fee or royalty for the right to use it.
SUP-08.Usage-based pricing: Customers are charged according to how much they actually use, like an electricity bill or pay-as-you-go phone data.
SUP-08.In-app purchases: An app or game is free or cheap to download, and users pay for extra content, features or virtual goods inside it.
SUP-08.Ticket sales: Customers pay an admission charge to enter or attend something, such as a concert, game, movie theater or theme park.
SUP-08.Affiliate marketing: The business promotes other companies' products and is paid a commission each time someone it refers makes a purchase.
SUP-08.Sponsorship: A company pays to have its name linked with an event, team, show or creator in order to reach that audience.
SUP-08.Razor and blades: The main product is sold cheaply, sometimes at a loss, and the profit comes from the refills customers must keep buying, like blades or printer ink.
SUP-08.Interest: The business lends money or lets customers pay over time, and earns the interest charged on what is owed, as banks and lenders do.
SUP-08.Auction: Buyers bid against each other and the item goes to the highest bidder, so the price is set by competition among buyers.
SUP-08.Listing fees: Sellers pay a platform a charge to post their item, job or property where buyers can find it, whether or not it sells.
SUP-08.Donations: People give money voluntarily to support the work, without receiving a product in return. Charities and some free services rely on this.
SUP-08.Pay what you want: Customers choose the price themselves, sometimes above a set minimum. It relies on buyers' goodwill and sense of fairness.
SUP-08.Data licensing: The business earns money by selling or licensing the information it has collected to other companies, within privacy laws.
SUP-08.Service contracts: Customers pay a regular or upfront fee for ongoing maintenance, support or repairs on a product they have bought, such as an extended warranty.

FND-01.Problem: The customer pain or unmet need the business exists to solve. A pitch starts here so investors see why the product matters.
FND-01.Solution: The product or service and how it fixes the problem, often shown with a demonstration or prototype.
FND-01.Market size: How many customers have the problem and how much they could spend. Investors want a market big enough to support a large business.
FND-01.Business model: How the company makes money: who pays, for what, and at what price.
FND-01.Team: The founders and key people, with the skills and experience that show they can carry out the plan. Investors often say they back people first.
FND-01.Competition: Who else is solving the same problem and how this business compares. Claiming to have no competitors is a warning sign to investors.
FND-01.Financial projections: Forecasts of sales, costs and profit for the next few years, with the assumptions behind them.
FND-01.The ask: The specific request: how much money the founders want and what they offer in return, such as a percentage of ownership.
FND-01.Hook: An opening line, fact or question that grabs attention in the first seconds and makes the audience want to hear more.
FND-01.Traction: Evidence that the idea is already working, such as early sales, signed-up users, pilot customers or growth figures.
FND-01.Go-to-market strategy: The plan for reaching the first customers and growing sales: which customers, through which channels, at what cost.
FND-01.Competitive advantage: What the business does better or differently that rivals cannot easily copy, such as a patent, lower costs or a unique feature.
FND-01.Vision: The long-term picture of what the company aims to become and the change it hopes to make.
FND-01.Use of funds: A breakdown of what the investment will be spent on, such as product development, hiring and marketing.
FND-01.Exit strategy: How investors are expected to get their money back with a profit, usually by the company being sold or listing its shares publicly.
FND-01.Roadmap: A timeline of the main milestones ahead, such as launch dates, new features and expansion into new markets.
FND-01.Valuation: What the founders say the company is worth today, which sets how much ownership an investor receives for the money put in.
FND-01.Story: A personal or customer story that makes the problem real and memorable and shows why the founders care about it.
FND-01.Closing: The final part of the pitch, which sums up the key points, repeats the request and invites questions or a next step.
FND-01.Why now: The reason this is the right moment for the business, such as a new technology, a change in the law or a shift in customer behavior.
FND-01.Risks: An honest account of what could go wrong and how the team plans to reduce or handle each danger.
FND-01.Intellectual property: Patents, trademarks, copyrights or trade secrets the company owns, which protect its idea from being copied.
FND-01.Unit economics: The revenue and cost tied to a single customer or sale, such as the cost to win a customer compared with what that customer is worth.

FND-02.Credit score: A number, based on past borrowing and repayment, that sums up how reliably a person or business has paid its debts. Lenders check the owner's and the firm's.
FND-02.Collateral: Property such as a building, equipment or inventory pledged to the lender, which the lender can take and sell if the loan is not repaid.
FND-02.Business plan: The written document describing the business, its market and its finances. It shows the lender how the money will be used and repaid.
FND-02.Financial statements: The income statement, balance sheet and related reports, which show the lender what the business earns, owns and owes.
FND-02.Cash flow: The money coming into and going out of the business. A lender wants to see enough cash arriving regularly to cover the loan payments.
FND-02.Capacity: One of the five Cs of credit: the borrower's ability to repay, judged by comparing income and cash flow with existing and new debt payments.
FND-02.Character: One of the five Cs of credit: the borrower's reputation for honesty and for paying debts, judged from credit history, references and background.
FND-02.Capital: One of the five Cs of credit: how much of their own money the owners have invested. Lenders trust borrowers who share the risk.
FND-02.Existing debt: What the business and owner already owe. Too much debt compared with income or equity leaves little room for another payment.
FND-02.Bank statements: Records of the deposits, withdrawals and balances in the business accounts, which confirm the sales and cash the owner claims.
FND-02.Financial projections: Forecasts of future sales, costs and cash flow, which show whether the business expects to earn enough to repay the loan.
FND-02.Loan amount: How much the business wants to borrow. The lender checks that the sum is reasonable for the purpose and for what the business can repay.
FND-02.Conditions: One of the five Cs of credit: the purpose of the loan and outside factors such as the state of the economy and of the industry.
FND-02.Tax returns: The income tax forms filed by the business and the owner for recent years, which lenders use to verify reported income.
FND-02.Time in business: How long the business has been operating. A longer record of survival makes a loan less risky, so startups find borrowing harder.
FND-02.Industry experience: The owner's and managers' background in this kind of business. Lenders have more confidence in people who know the industry.
FND-02.Legal documents: Papers proving the business is properly set up and what it has agreed to, such as licenses, articles of incorporation, leases and contracts.
FND-02.Personal financial statement: A list of what the owner personally owns and owes. Lenders ask for it because small business owners often back the loan themselves.
FND-02.Debt service coverage ratio: Operating income divided by the loan payments due in the same period. A ratio above 1 means the business earns more than enough to make its payments.
FND-02.Personal guarantee: The owner's written promise to repay the loan from personal assets if the business cannot. A cosigner makes a similar promise for someone else.
FND-02.Accounts receivable aging: A report that sorts the money customers owe the business by how long each invoice has been unpaid. Old unpaid invoices may never be collected.
FND-02.Insurance coverage: Proof that the business and any pledged property are insured, so that a fire or lawsuit would not wipe out its ability to repay.

FND-03.Work from home: Running the business from the owner's house or garage, which avoids paying rent, deposits and utilities for a separate space.
FND-03.Buy used equipment: Purchasing secondhand or refurbished machines and furniture, which usually cost far less than new ones and do the same job.
FND-03.Lease equipment: Renting equipment for a regular payment instead of buying it, which swaps a large upfront cost for smaller monthly ones.
FND-03.Keep a day job: Staying employed while starting the business part time, so the founder's wages cover living costs and the business needs less cash.
FND-03.Cut unnecessary expenses: Spending only on what the business truly needs to open and leaving out extras such as a fancy office or premium fittings.
FND-03.Hire freelancers: Paying independent workers by the task or hour, for jobs such as design or bookkeeping, instead of taking on full-time employees.
FND-03.Share space: Splitting premises with others, for example in a coworking office, a shared commercial kitchen or a sublet corner of another shop.
FND-03.Use free software: Choosing free or open-source programs and free website builders instead of paying for licenses and custom development.
FND-03.Take no salary: The founders work without pay at first, or do jobs themselves that they would otherwise pay for. The unpaid work is called sweat equity.
FND-03.Start small: Launching with a limited version, such as one product or a basic model, and expanding only once sales prove the idea.
FND-03.Sell online only: Opening as an internet store with no physical shop, which removes the cost of rent, fittings and shop staff.
FND-03.Hire fewer employees: Opening with a very small team or part-time workers, and adding staff only when sales can pay for them.
FND-03.Choose a cheaper location: Picking a smaller space or a less expensive area, accepting a less prominent site in return for lower rent.
FND-03.Pre-sell: Taking orders and deposits before the product exists, so customers' payments fund the first production run.
FND-03.Barter: Trading goods or services directly for other goods or services, with no cash changing hands, such as design work in exchange for printing.
FND-03.Use low-cost marketing: Promoting the business through cheap or free methods such as social media, word of mouth and creative stunts instead of paid advertising.
FND-03.Negotiate supplier terms: Asking suppliers for lower prices or more time to pay. Buying now and paying in 30 or 60 days is called trade credit.
FND-03.Drop shipping: Selling products that a supplier stores and ships directly to the customer, so the seller never has to buy inventory in advance.
FND-03.Hire interns: Using students or trainees who work for experience, course credit or low pay, within labor law, to get help cheaply.
FND-03.Join an incubator: Entering a program that gives new businesses cheap or free office space, shared services and advice while they get started.
FND-03.Start with a pop-up or truck: Opening in a temporary stall, kiosk or food truck, which costs far less than fitting out a permanent store.
FND-03.Borrow equipment: Using tools or machines lent by friends, family or another business instead of paying to buy or rent them.
FND-03.Keep inventory low: Holding only a small amount of stock, or making items only when ordered, so less money is tied up in unsold goods.
FND-03.Consignment: Stocking goods that still belong to the supplier and paying for each item only after it has been sold to a customer.
FND-03.Use free advice: Getting guidance from free services such as SCORE mentors and Small Business Development Centers instead of paying consultants.

FND-04.Term loan: A lump sum borrowed from a bank or credit union and repaid with interest in regular installments over a fixed period.
FND-04.Line of credit: An agreed borrowing limit the business can draw on, repay and draw on again as needed, paying interest only on the amount in use.
FND-04.SBA loan: A loan from a bank or other lender that is partly guaranteed by the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA), reducing the lender's risk.
FND-04.Business credit card: A card that lets the business buy now and pay later. It is convenient for small purchases but charges high interest on unpaid balances.
FND-04.Microloan: A small loan, typically up to about $50,000, from a nonprofit or community lender, aimed at very small or new businesses.
FND-04.Equipment loan: A loan used to buy machinery or vehicles, in which the equipment itself serves as the security for the loan.
FND-04.Personal loan: A loan taken out in the owner's own name, based on personal credit, with the money then used in the business.
FND-04.Loan from friends or family: Money lent by people the owner knows personally, often on easy terms. It should still be put in writing to avoid disputes.
FND-04.Secured loan: A loan backed by collateral, property the lender may take if the borrower fails to repay. This lowers the risk and usually the interest rate.
FND-04.Commercial mortgage: A long-term loan used to buy business property such as a shop, office or warehouse, with the property as security.
FND-04.Trade credit: Credit given by a supplier that lets the business receive goods now and pay later, commonly within 30 days.
FND-04.Home equity loan: A loan secured by the owner's home, based on the value the owner has built up in it. Failure to repay puts the home at risk.
FND-04.Unsecured loan: A loan with no collateral behind it, granted on the borrower's credit record alone, so it usually carries a higher interest rate.
FND-04.Working capital loan: A short-term loan to cover everyday running costs such as wages, rent and inventory, not to buy long-term assets.
FND-04.Invoice factoring: Selling unpaid customer invoices to a finance company, called a factor, at a discount in order to receive cash immediately.
FND-04.Merchant cash advance: A lump sum given in return for a share of the business's future card sales, collected daily. It is fast but usually very expensive.
FND-04.Peer-to-peer loan: A loan arranged through an online platform that connects the borrower with individuals or investors who fund it, instead of a bank.
FND-04.Bonds: Debt sold to investors: the issuer promises to pay interest and return the amount borrowed on a set date. Mostly used by large companies.
FND-04.Promissory note: A signed written promise to repay a stated sum, with interest, by a given date. It is the basic legal document behind many loans.
FND-04.Inventory financing: A loan or credit line used to buy stock, with that stock as collateral. Car dealers use a form called floor plan financing.
FND-04.Bridge loan: A short-term loan that covers a gap until longer-term financing or an expected payment arrives.
FND-04.Convertible note: A loan from an investor that is designed to convert into shares of the company at a later funding round instead of being repaid in cash.
FND-04.Venture debt: Loans made to startups that already have venture capital backing, giving them extra cash without selling much more ownership.
FND-04.Purchase order financing: A lender pays the supplier so the business can fill a large confirmed customer order, and is repaid when the customer pays.
FND-04.Construction loan: A short-term loan that pays for building or renovating premises, with the money released in stages as the work is completed.
FND-04.Disaster loan: A low-interest government loan, in the U.S. from the Small Business Administration, that helps businesses recover from a declared disaster.

FND-05.Venture capital: Money that professional firms invest in young, fast-growing companies in exchange for shares, pooled from outside investors.
FND-05.Valuation: The value placed on a company for an investment. Pre-money is the value before the new money goes in, and post-money is the value after.
FND-05.Angel investor: A wealthy individual who invests personal money in a startup at a very early stage, in return for a share of ownership.
FND-05.Funding round: One stage of raising money from investors. Rounds are named in order, such as seed, Series A and Series B, as the company grows.
FND-05.Ownership stake: The percentage of a company that a person or investor owns, usually held as shares.
FND-05.Dilution: The fall in each existing owner's percentage of the company when new shares are issued to new investors.
FND-05.Term sheet: A short document setting out the main terms of a proposed investment, such as the amount, the valuation and the investors' rights. Most of it is not binding.
FND-05.Due diligence: The investor's careful check of a company's finances, legal position, product and team before the investment is completed.
FND-05.Exit: The event that lets founders and investors turn their shares into cash, usually the sale of the company or an initial public offering.
FND-05.Pitch deck: A short slide presentation founders use to explain their business to possible investors.
FND-05.Return on investment: The gain an investor makes compared with the amount invested. Startup investors often describe it as a multiple of their money.
FND-05.Private equity: Investment funds that buy large stakes in, or all of, established private companies, aiming to improve them and sell at a profit.
FND-05.Equity crowdfunding: Raising money online from a large number of people who each receive a small ownership share in the company.
FND-05.Cap table: Short for capitalization table: a list of everyone who owns part of the company and how much each holds.
FND-05.Vesting: Earning shares or options gradually over time. A founder or employee who leaves early keeps only the part already vested.
FND-05.Preferred stock: The class of shares investors usually receive, carrying extra rights that common stock lacks, such as being paid first if the company is sold.
FND-05.Common stock: The basic class of shares, usually held by founders and employees. It has voting rights but is paid after preferred stock in a sale.
FND-05.Stock options: The right to buy company shares later at a price fixed today. Startups grant them to employees as part of their pay.
FND-05.Accelerator: A fixed-length program that gives early startups a small investment, mentoring and investor contacts, usually in return for a small ownership stake.
FND-05.Unicorn: A privately held startup valued at one billion dollars or more.
FND-05.Convertible note: A short-term loan to a startup that converts into shares at a later funding round, usually at a discount to the price new investors pay.
FND-05.Liquidation preference: A term giving investors the right to be paid back, often the amount they invested, before common shareholders if the company is sold or closed.
FND-05.Board seat: A place on the company's board of directors, which lets an investor vote on major decisions. Lead investors often require one.
FND-05.Lead investor: The investor who puts in the largest share of a round, negotiates the terms with the company and is followed by the other investors.
FND-05.Accredited investor: A person or institution that meets legal tests of income, wealth or expertise and so is allowed to buy investments not registered for public sale.
FND-05.Shareholder agreement: A contract among a company's owners setting out their rights and duties, such as how shares can be sold and how decisions are made.
FND-05.Sweat equity: Ownership earned through unpaid work instead of money, such as founders who build the company without taking a salary.
FND-05.SAFE: A simple agreement for future equity: the investor pays now and receives shares at a later funding round. Unlike a note, it is not a loan and has no interest.
FND-05.Pro rata rights: An investor's right to buy enough shares in later rounds to keep the same percentage of ownership.
FND-05.Anti-dilution protection: A term that adjusts an investor's shares in their favor if the company later sells shares at a lower price than they paid.
FND-05.Down round: A funding round in which shares are sold at a lower valuation than in the previous round.
FND-05.Valuation cap: The highest company valuation at which a convertible note or SAFE will convert into shares, protecting early investors if the value soars.
FND-05.Drag-along rights: A term letting majority owners force minority owners to join in a sale of the company. Tag-along rights let minority owners join a sale on the same terms.
FND-05.Warrants: Rights, often given to lenders or investors, to buy a company's shares at a set price for a set period.
FND-05.Carried interest: The share of a fund's profits, commonly about 20 percent, that goes to the fund's managers as their reward for good results.
FND-05.Limited partner: An investor who supplies money to a venture capital fund, such as a pension fund or wealthy person, but takes no part in running it.
FND-05.General partner: A manager of a venture capital fund, who chooses which startups to invest in and is responsible for running the fund.
FND-05.Portfolio company: A company that a venture capital or private equity fund has invested in.

FND-06.Revenue growth: How fast sales are rising from one period to the next, usually given as a percentage per month or year.
FND-06.Profit margin: The share of each dollar of sales that is left as profit after costs, shown as a percentage. Gross margin counts only the direct cost of the goods.
FND-06.Customer acquisition cost: The average amount spent on marketing and sales to win one new customer: total acquisition spending divided by new customers gained.
FND-06.Burn rate: How much cash a startup spends each month beyond what it brings in. A high burn rate uses up the money raised from investors quickly.
FND-06.Number of customers: A count of the people buying or using the product, such as paying customers or monthly active users, tracked to show growth.
FND-06.Churn rate: The percentage of customers who stop buying or cancel during a period. High churn means the business must keep replacing lost customers.
FND-06.Customer lifetime value: The total profit or revenue a business expects to earn from an average customer over the whole time they stay a customer.
FND-06.Runway: The number of months a startup can keep operating before its cash runs out: cash in the bank divided by the monthly burn rate.
FND-06.Cash flow: The money actually moving into and out of the business in a period. Positive cash flow means more came in than went out.
FND-06.Return on investment: The profit earned compared with the money put in, shown as a percentage. It tells owners and investors how well their money is working.
FND-06.Monthly recurring revenue: The predictable income a subscription business receives every month from its current subscribers.
FND-06.Retention rate: The percentage of customers who keep buying or stay subscribed over a period. It is the opposite of churn.
FND-06.Break-even point: The level of sales at which total revenue equals total costs, so the business makes neither a profit nor a loss.
FND-06.Market share: The business's portion of all the sales in its market, shown as a percentage.
FND-06.Conversion rate: The percentage of people who take a desired action, such as website visitors who go on to make a purchase.
FND-06.Valuation: What the whole company is judged to be worth, usually set when investors buy shares. A rising valuation signals progress.
FND-06.Average revenue per user: Total revenue divided by the number of users or customers in a period, showing how much each one brings in.
FND-06.Net promoter score: A measure of customer loyalty based on asking how likely customers are, from 0 to 10, to recommend the business to others.
FND-06.Website traffic: The number of visits or visitors to the company's website, an early sign of interest for an online business.
FND-06.Engagement: How actively people use a product, for example how often they open an app and how long they spend in it.
FND-06.Current ratio: Current assets divided by current liabilities. It shows whether the business has enough short-term resources to pay the bills due within a year.
FND-06.Debt-to-equity ratio: Total debt divided by owners' equity. It shows how much the business relies on borrowed money compared with the owners' money.
FND-06.Average order value: Total revenue divided by the number of orders, giving the typical amount a customer spends per purchase.
FND-06.LTV to CAC ratio: Customer lifetime value (LTV) divided by customer acquisition cost (CAC). It shows whether a customer is worth more than it costs to win one.
FND-06.Payback period: The time it takes for the money earned from a customer or an investment to cover what was spent to obtain it.
FND-06.Net revenue retention: The revenue this period from customers the company already had a year ago, as a percentage of what they paid then, counting upgrades and cancellations.
FND-06.Gross merchandise value: The total dollar value of everything sold through a marketplace in a period, before the platform takes out its own fees.
FND-06.Contribution margin: The selling price of one unit minus its variable costs: the amount each sale contributes toward fixed costs and profit.

FND-07.Income statement: A report of revenue, expenses and the resulting profit or loss over a period. It is also called a profit and loss statement.
FND-07.Cash flow statement: A report of the cash expected to come in and go out, usually month by month, showing whether the business can pay its bills on time.
FND-07.Balance sheet: A snapshot at one date of what the business owns (assets), what it owes (liabilities) and the owners' share (equity).
FND-07.Sales forecast: An estimate of how much the business expects to sell in future months and years. The other projections are built on it.
FND-07.Break-even analysis: A calculation of the sales needed for revenue to cover all costs exactly. Beyond that point the business starts to make a profit.
FND-07.Pro forma statements: Projected financial statements that show what the income statement, balance sheet and cash flow are expected to look like in future periods.
FND-07.Startup costs: A list of everything that must be paid for before the business opens, such as equipment, deposits, licenses and opening inventory.
FND-07.Budget: A plan of expected income and spending for a coming period, used to control costs and compare with actual results.
FND-07.Funding request: A statement of how much money the business is asking for, in what form, and on what terms it would be repaid or rewarded.
FND-07.Assumptions: The estimates behind the projections, such as prices, growth rates and costs, written out so a reader can judge whether the numbers are realistic.
FND-07.Ratio analysis: Calculations that compare figures from the financial statements, such as the current ratio or profit margin, to judge financial health.
FND-07.Personal financial statement: A list of what each owner personally owns and owes. Lenders ask for it because owners of small firms often guarantee the loan.
FND-07.Capital expenditure budget: A plan for spending on long-lasting assets such as equipment, vehicles and buildings.
FND-07.Historical financial statements: The actual financial statements from past years, included when the business already exists so readers can see its record.
FND-07.Statement of owners equity: A report showing how the owners' stake changed during a period through investments, profit or loss, and withdrawals.
FND-07.Sources and uses of funds: A table showing where the startup money will come from, such as loans and owner investment, and exactly what it will be spent on.
FND-07.Loan repayment schedule: A table of each loan payment over the life of the loan, showing how much is interest and how much reduces the amount owed.
FND-07.Sensitivity analysis: A test of how the results change if key assumptions turn out differently, such as best-case and worst-case sales.
FND-07.Personnel budget: A projection of the jobs the business will fill and what the wages, payroll taxes and benefits will cost.

SBM-01.Lack of capital: Starting or running with too little money, called undercapitalization, so the business cannot cover its costs until sales grow.
SBM-01.Poor management: Owners who lack the skills to plan, lead people and make sound decisions. It is one of the most commonly cited causes of failure.
SBM-01.Cash flow problems: Money comes in later than bills fall due, so the business cannot pay suppliers, staff or rent even if it is profitable on paper.
SBM-01.No market need: Too few people want the product at the price asked, so sales never reach the level needed to cover costs.
SBM-01.Competition: Rivals, often larger ones with lower prices or bigger budgets, take the customers the small business depends on.
SBM-01.Poor location: A site with too little customer traffic, poor visibility or the wrong kind of neighborhood for the business.
SBM-01.Lack of planning: Opening without a realistic business plan, so problems with costs, customers or competitors are not seen until they hit.
SBM-01.Lack of experience: The owner does not know the industry or the basics of running a business, and makes mistakes an experienced owner would avoid.
SBM-01.Poor marketing: Customers never hear about the business, or the message reaches the wrong people, so sales stay low.
SBM-01.Too much debt: Loan payments take so much of the income that there is not enough left to run the business or survive a slow period.
SBM-01.High costs: Spending on rent, staff, stock or extras is greater than the sales can support, wiping out any profit.
SBM-01.Pricing problems: Prices set too low to cover costs and leave a profit, or so high that customers go elsewhere.
SBM-01.Growing too fast: Expanding before the money, staff and systems are ready. The cost of new stock, people and space arrives before the extra sales do.
SBM-01.Poor customer service: Customers who are treated badly do not return and warn others away, so the business loses repeat sales.
SBM-01.Poor hiring: Choosing unsuitable employees, or losing good ones, which hurts service and quality and raises costs.
SBM-01.Failure to adapt: Continuing with the same products and methods while customers' tastes, technology and competitors change.
SBM-01.No competitive advantage: The business offers nothing that customers cannot get just as well elsewhere, so they have no reason to choose it.
SBM-01.Economic downturn: A recession or other slump in which customers cut spending. Small firms have thin cash reserves and may not outlast it.
SBM-01.Poor inventory management: Holding too much stock, which ties up cash and may spoil or go out of date, or too little, which loses sales.
SBM-01.Owner burnout: The owner becomes exhausted by long hours and constant stress and can no longer run the business well.
SBM-01.Partner conflict: Serious disagreements between co-owners about money, workload or direction that paralyze or split the business.
SBM-01.Theft and fraud: Losses from shoplifting, break-ins, dishonest employees or scams, which a small firm may be unable to absorb.
SBM-01.Legal problems: Lawsuits, fines or broken regulations that bring costs the business cannot afford or force it to stop operating.
SBM-01.Poor record keeping: Incomplete or inaccurate financial records, so the owner does not know the true sales, costs and debts until it is too late.
SBM-01.Poor credit management: Letting customers buy on credit too freely and failing to collect what they owe, so sales are made but the cash never arrives.
SBM-01.Dependence on one customer: Most of the sales come from a single buyer, so losing that one account can destroy the business.
SBM-01.Uninsured disaster: A fire, flood or similar event causes a loss that the business has no insurance, or too little, to cover.
SBM-01.Tax problems: Failing to set money aside for taxes or to file correctly, leading to back taxes, penalties and interest.
SBM-01.Owner takes out too much money: The owner draws more cash for personal use than the business can spare, leaving too little to pay bills and reinvest.

SBM-02.Small Business Administration: The federal agency that supports small firms by guaranteeing loans made by lenders, funding counseling programs and helping them win government contracts.
SBM-02.Chamber of commerce: A local association of businesses that promotes the area's business community and offers its members networking, publicity and a voice with local government.
SBM-02.SCORE: A nonprofit partner of the Small Business Administration whose volunteer mentors, many of them retired executives, give free advice to owners.
SBM-02.Small Business Development Center: One of a national network of centers, often at colleges and partly funded by the Small Business Administration, giving free consulting and low-cost training.
SBM-02.Business incubator: An organization that helps very new businesses get started by providing low-cost space, shared services, advice and contacts.
SBM-02.Accelerator: A short, competitive program that gives young startups mentoring, contacts and often a small investment to speed up their growth.
SBM-02.Banks and credit unions: Financial institutions that provide business accounts, loans and lines of credit, and often advice on managing money.
SBM-02.Trade association: An organization of businesses in the same industry that shares information, training and standards and speaks for its members.
SBM-02.Better Business Bureau: A private nonprofit that rates businesses on trustworthiness, handles customer complaints and accredits firms that meet its standards.
SBM-02.Womens Business Center: One of a national network of centers, funded partly by the Small Business Administration, that offers training and counseling aimed at women entrepreneurs.
SBM-02.Minority Business Development Agency: A federal agency within the Department of Commerce that helps minority-owned businesses grow through its business centers and access to capital and contracts.
SBM-02.Economic development agency: A state or local body that works to attract and grow businesses in its area, offering help such as site information, incentives and loans.
SBM-02.Nonprofit microlender: A nonprofit organization that makes very small loans to entrepreneurs who cannot get bank credit, often with coaching included.
SBM-02.College entrepreneurship center: A program at a college or university that teaches entrepreneurship and gives students and local founders advice, workspace and contacts.
SBM-02.Business networking group: A group of local business people who meet regularly to exchange contacts, referrals and advice.
SBM-02.National Federation of Independent Busin: A membership association that lobbies government on behalf of small and independent business owners.
SBM-02.Veterans Business Outreach Center: A Small Business Administration program that gives military veterans, service members and their spouses training and counseling for starting a business.
SBM-02.Small Business Investment Company: A privately owned investment fund licensed by the Small Business Administration, which uses its own money plus government-backed funds to invest in small firms.
SBM-02.Community development financial institut: A lender certified by the U.S. Treasury whose mission is to provide loans in low-income communities that mainstream banks often do not serve.
SBM-02.Small Business Innovation Research progr: A federal program in which government agencies award competitive grants and contracts to small firms to develop new technology.
