GRO-03.Foreign distributor: An independent firm in the foreign country that buys or handles the product and resells it there, using its own local contacts.
GRO-03.Contract manufacturing: Paying a manufacturer in the foreign country to produce the goods, which the firm then markets itself under its own brand.
GRO-03.Foreign sales office: A branch the company opens abroad, staffed by its own people, to promote and sell products made elsewhere.
GRO-03.Management contract: The firm supplies managers and know-how to run an operation, such as a hotel, that a foreign owner has paid for, and receives a fee.
GRO-03.Turnkey project: The firm designs, builds and equips a facility abroad, such as a power plant, then hands it over to the local owner ready to operate.
GRO-03.Piggybacking: A company sells its products abroad through the established export channels of another firm that already operates there.
GRO-03.Countertrade: Selling to a foreign buyer and being paid wholly or partly in goods or services instead of money. Barter is its simplest form.

GRO-04.Earnings multiple: The value is set as the yearly profit times a number typical for the industry. A firm earning $100,000 at a multiple of 3 is worth $300,000.
GRO-04.Asset-based valuation: The value is taken as what the business owns minus what it owes, using the worth of its assets adjusted to current values.
GRO-04.Comparable sales: The value is estimated from the prices recently paid for similar businesses, as houses are priced from nearby sales. Also called the market approach.
GRO-04.Discounted cash flow: The value is the total of the cash the business is expected to produce in future years, each amount reduced to what it is worth today.
GRO-04.Revenue multiple: The value is set as the yearly sales times a number typical for the industry. It is used when profits are small or unreliable.
GRO-04.Market capitalization: For a company with publicly traded shares, the share price multiplied by the number of shares in existence.
GRO-04.Goodwill and intangibles: The value of things that cannot be touched, such as reputation, brand and loyal customers. Goodwill is what a buyer pays above the value of the other assets.
GRO-04.Professional appraisal: An estimate of value prepared by an independent, qualified business appraiser, who usually applies several methods.
GRO-04.Liquidation value: The amount that would be left if the business closed, sold its assets quickly and paid its debts. It is usually the lowest valuation.
GRO-04.Replacement cost: The value is taken as what it would cost today to build an equivalent business from scratch, with the same assets.
GRO-04.Enterprise value: The value of the whole business to all who finance it: the value of its equity plus its debt, minus its cash.
GRO-04.Growth rate: How fast sales and profits are rising. A business that is growing quickly is worth a higher multiple than one that is flat.
GRO-04.Return on investment: The yearly profit the buyer would earn as a percentage of the price paid. Buyers work back from the return they require to a price.
GRO-04.Capitalization of earnings: The value is the expected yearly earnings divided by a capitalization rate, the rate of return a buyer requires for the risk.
GRO-04.Seller discretionary earnings: A small firm's profit before the owner's pay, perks, interest and one-off items: the total benefit a single working owner receives.
GRO-04.Rule of thumb: A quick formula commonly used in a particular industry, such as a set percentage of yearly sales. It gives only a rough estimate.
GRO-04.Excess earnings method: Tangible assets are valued first. Any earnings above a normal return on those assets are then turned into a value for goodwill and added.
GRO-04.Venture capital method: Used for startups: estimate what the company could sell for in a future year, then work back to today using the high return investors require.
GRO-04.First Chicago method: The business is valued under best, expected and worst-case scenarios, and the results are averaged, weighted by how likely each is.

GRO-05.Cash shortages: Growth costs money before it earns any: extra stock, staff and space must be paid for ahead of the sales, so cash can run out.
GRO-05.Hiring enough staff: The business needs more workers than it can find and train in time, and hiring in a hurry leads to poor choices.
GRO-05.Quality slips: Rushing to make or deliver more, with new and stretched staff, causes more mistakes and uneven products.
GRO-05.Customer service suffers: Staff are too busy to give each customer proper attention, so waits get longer and complaints rise.
GRO-05.Inventory shortages: Demand outruns what the business and its suppliers can provide, so items go out of stock and orders are late.
GRO-05.Outgrowing the space: The premises become too small for the extra stock, staff and customers, and moving or expanding is costly and disruptive.
GRO-05.Owner must delegate: The owner can no longer do or supervise everything personally and must hand tasks and decisions to others, which many find difficult.
GRO-05.Higher costs: Expenses such as wages, rent and equipment climb with expansion and can rise faster than the sales that are meant to pay for them.
GRO-05.More debt: The business borrows heavily to pay for expansion, and the repayments become a burden if sales do not grow as planned.
GRO-05.Burnout: The owner and staff work long hours under pressure to keep up, becoming exhausted and less effective.
GRO-05.Weak systems: Informal methods that worked for a small firm, such as simple record keeping, cannot cope with a much larger volume of business.
GRO-05.Communication breakdown: With more people and departments, information no longer passes easily to everyone, causing mistakes and confusion.
GRO-05.Loss of company culture: The values and close team spirit of the small firm weaken as many new people join quickly.
GRO-05.Need for more managers: A bigger workforce needs supervisors and a clear management structure, which the business may lack experienced people to fill.
GRO-05.Training gaps: New employees are put to work before they have been properly taught the job, because there is no time to train them.
GRO-05.Lower profit margins: Profit per dollar of sales falls, because costs rise quickly or prices are cut to win the extra business.
GRO-05.Employee turnover: Overworked or unhappy staff leave, and the business loses experience just when it most needs it.
GRO-05.Increased competition: Visible success attracts rivals into the market and draws a stronger response from existing competitors.
GRO-05.Loss of personal touch: The owner can no longer know every customer, so service becomes less personal than the business was known for.
GRO-05.More regulation: Passing certain sizes, such as a set number of employees, brings the business under laws that did not apply when it was smaller.
GRO-05.Loss of focus: Chasing too many new opportunities at once pulls the business away from what it does best.
GRO-05.Slow collection of receivables: More sales on credit mean more money owed by customers, and the cash is tied up until they pay.
GRO-05.Ownership dilution: Selling shares to investors to pay for growth leaves the founders owning a smaller percentage of the company and with less control.

GRO-06.Language barriers: Customers, staff and officials speak a different language, so labels, ads and contracts must be translated accurately and misunderstandings are easy.
GRO-06.Cultural differences: Customs, values, manners and ways of doing business differ, so products or behavior that are normal at home may offend or fail.
GRO-06.Tariffs: Taxes a government charges on imported goods, which raise the price of the product in the foreign market.
GRO-06.Exchange rates: The value of one currency against another keeps changing, so the amount a foreign sale is worth at home can fall after the price is agreed.
GRO-06.Different laws: Each country has its own rules on matters such as contracts, employment, product safety and advertising, which the business must learn and obey.
GRO-06.Shipping costs: Moving goods over long distances is expensive and slow, and longer supply chains have more points where things can go wrong.
GRO-06.Political instability: Unrest, war or sudden changes of government can disrupt business, and a government may even seize foreign-owned property.
GRO-06.Lack of market knowledge: The business does not know the foreign customers, competitors and buying habits as it does those at home, so mistakes are likely.
GRO-06.High cost: Entering another country takes a large investment in research, travel, legal advice, marketing and facilities before any sales are made.
GRO-06.Different customer tastes: Foreign customers may want different flavors, sizes, features or styles, so the product has to be adapted.
GRO-06.Local competition: Established firms in the country already know the market and have loyal customers and distribution in place.
GRO-06.Time zones: Working hours do not overlap across distant countries, making meetings, customer support and quick decisions harder.
GRO-06.Hiring local staff: The business must find, employ and manage qualified workers in a country whose job market and labor rules it does not know.
GRO-06.Economic conditions: Incomes, inflation and economic stability differ from home, affecting what customers can afford and how risky the market is.
GRO-06.Trade restrictions: Government limits on trade other than tariffs, such as quotas on quantities, import licenses and bans called embargoes.
GRO-06.Customs paperwork: The documents and inspections required to move goods across a border, which cause delays and fines if done wrongly.
GRO-06.Getting paid: Collecting money from buyers in another country is harder, because pursuing a customer who does not pay across borders is slow and costly.
GRO-06.Poor infrastructure: Roads, ports, electricity or internet in the country may be unreliable, making it hard to produce, deliver and communicate.
GRO-06.Foreign taxes: The business must understand and pay another country's taxes, and its profits may be taxed both there and at home.
GRO-06.Managing from a distance: It is hard to supervise operations, keep standards up and solve problems quickly in a place far from head office.
GRO-06.Lack of brand recognition: Customers in the new country have never heard of the business, so it must build its name and trust from the beginning.
GRO-06.Adapting the marketing: Brand names, ads, packaging and prices that work at home may need changing to suit the new country's language, culture and laws.
GRO-06.Finding local partners: The business needs trustworthy distributors, suppliers or agents in the country, and they are hard to find and check from abroad.
GRO-06.Intellectual property theft: In countries where patents, trademarks and copyrights are weakly enforced, products and brands may be copied or counterfeited.
GRO-06.Corruption: Officials in some countries expect bribes. Paying them is illegal for U.S. firms under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, and refusing can cause delays.
GRO-06.Different technical standards: Rules on voltage, measurements, safety and labeling differ between countries, so products may need to be redesigned.
GRO-06.Repatriating profits: Some governments limit how much money earned in the country can be converted and sent back to the company's home country.
GRO-06.Consumer ethnocentrism: The belief among some consumers that buying foreign products is wrong or disloyal, leading them to prefer goods made at home.

ENT-08.Financial risk: The owner usually invests personal savings or borrowed money in the business and can lose some or all of it if the business does poorly.
ENT-08.Long hours: Owners often work far more than a normal work week, including evenings and weekends, especially while the business is new.
ENT-08.Uncertain income: An owner has no guaranteed paycheck. Income rises and falls with sales, and in the early months there may be none at all.
ENT-08.Stress: Worrying about money, customers, employees and deadlines puts constant pressure on a business owner.
ENT-08.Risk of failure: Many new businesses close within their first few years, so an entrepreneur must accept that the venture may not survive.
ENT-08.Full responsibility: The owner answers for every decision and every problem, from sales to bills to staffing, with no boss to pass them to.
ENT-08.No employee benefits: Nobody provides the owner with health insurance, paid vacation, sick pay or a retirement plan. The owner must pay for these personally.
ENT-08.Less time with family: The time and energy a business demands leave less for family, friends and hobbies, which can strain relationships.
ENT-08.Competition: Other businesses are always trying to win the same customers, and larger rivals may have more money and lower prices.
ENT-08.Personal liability: In a sole proprietorship or general partnership the owner is personally responsible for business debts and lawsuits, so a home or savings can be at risk.
ENT-08.No job security: An entrepreneur gives up the security of a steady job, and nobody guarantees that the business, or the work it provides, will still be there next year.
ENT-08.Difficulty getting financing: New owners with no track record often struggle to get loans or attract investors, so money for the business is hard to raise.
ENT-08.Loneliness: Many owners, especially those working alone, have no coworkers or boss to share problems and decisions with.
ENT-08.Paperwork and regulations: Owners must keep records, file taxes, get licenses and follow government rules, which takes time away from running the business.
ENT-08.Undesirable duties: Owners must handle tasks they dislike, such as firing an employee, chasing unpaid bills or cleaning up, because the job still has to be done.
ENT-08.Opportunity cost: What the entrepreneur gives up to start the business, such as the salary and career progress of a regular job.
ENT-08.Self-employment tax: A self-employed person pays both the employee share and the employer share of Social Security and Medicare taxes, which an employer would otherwise split.
ENT-08.Health effects: Long hours, stress and too little sleep can wear down an owner's physical and mental health over time.

ENT-09.Job creation: New and small businesses hire workers, and together they employ a large share of the people who work in the private sector.
ENT-09.Innovation: Entrepreneurs bring new products, services and ways of doing things to market, often faster than large established companies.
ENT-09.Competition: New businesses challenge existing ones, which pushes every firm to improve quality, service and prices.
ENT-09.Economic growth: The goods and services that new businesses produce add to gross domestic product (GDP), the total output of the economy.
ENT-09.Meeting needs and wants: Entrepreneurs spot what people need or want and supply the goods and services that satisfy them.
ENT-09.Tax revenue: Businesses and their employees pay income, payroll, sales and property taxes that help fund government services.
ENT-09.Consumer choice: More businesses mean more products, brands and stores for shoppers to choose between.
ENT-09.Lower prices: When new firms compete for customers, sellers are pushed to keep prices down, which helps consumers.
ENT-09.Community support: Local businesses spend and hire nearby, sponsor teams and events and give to local causes, which keeps money circulating in the community.
ENT-09.Wealth creation: A successful business produces income for its owners, wages for its workers and returns for its investors.
ENT-09.Higher standard of living: Jobs, incomes and better products raise the level of comfort and well-being that people in an economy enjoy.
ENT-09.Serving niche markets: Small businesses serve small or specialized groups of customers that are too limited to interest large companies.
ENT-09.Supplying larger businesses: Many small firms make parts or provide services for big companies, and they also buy from other businesses themselves.
ENT-09.Opportunities for women and minorities: Business ownership gives women, minorities, immigrants and others a path to economic independence and advancement.
ENT-09.Exports: Many small businesses sell goods and services to customers in other countries, which brings money into the home economy.
ENT-09.Productivity: New methods and technology from entrepreneurs let the economy produce more output from the same amount of resources.
ENT-09.Training workers: Small businesses give many people their first jobs, where they learn skills and work habits they carry through their careers.
ENT-09.Creative destruction: Joseph Schumpeter's term for the way new businesses and technologies replace outdated ones, moving resources to better uses.
ENT-09.Solving social problems: Social entrepreneurs start ventures aimed at problems such as poverty, health or pollution, not only at profit.

ENT-10.Retail: A business that sells goods directly to the final consumer, in a store or online. Examples are clothing shops and supermarkets.
ENT-10.Manufacturing: A business that turns raw materials or parts into finished goods, such as a furniture maker or a car plant.
ENT-10.Construction: A business that builds or repairs houses, offices, roads and other structures, such as a home builder or a roofing contractor.
ENT-10.Hospitality: A business that feeds, houses or hosts guests, such as a restaurant, hotel or catering company.
ENT-10.Health care: A business that provides medical care, such as a doctor's office, dental practice, clinic or home health agency.
ENT-10.Wholesale: A business that buys goods in large quantities from producers and resells them to retailers or other businesses, not to the public.
ENT-10.Agriculture: A business that grows crops or raises animals for food and other products, such as a farm, ranch or orchard.
ENT-10.Finance and insurance: A business that handles money or risk for customers, such as a bank, credit union, investment firm or insurance company.
ENT-10.Information and media: A business that produces or carries information, such as a publisher, broadcaster, software company or telephone and internet provider.
ENT-10.Mining and extraction: A business that takes raw materials such as coal, metal ores, stone, oil or natural gas out of the earth.
ENT-10.Transportation: A business that moves people or goods from place to place, such as a trucking company, airline or delivery service.
ENT-10.Real estate: A business that sells, rents or manages land and buildings, such as a real estate brokerage or an apartment management company.
ENT-10.Education: A business that teaches or trains people for a fee, such as a tutoring center, private school or driving school.
ENT-10.Professional services: A business that sells specialized expert knowledge to clients, such as a law firm, an accounting firm, an engineering company or a consulting firm.
ENT-10.Entertainment and recreation: A business that provides fun or leisure activities, such as a movie theater, sports team, gym or amusement park.
ENT-10.Forestry and fishing: A business that harvests timber from forests or catches fish and seafood. Like mining, it takes raw materials from nature.
ENT-10.Utilities: A business that supplies basic services such as electricity, natural gas or water to homes and other businesses.
ENT-10.Personal services: A business that does everyday jobs for individuals and their belongings, such as a hair salon, a dry cleaner or an auto repair shop.
ENT-10.Waste management: A business that collects, hauls away, recycles or disposes of trash and other waste for households and companies.
ENT-10.Administrative and support services: A business that handles day-to-day support work for other businesses, such as a staffing agency, a janitorial company, a security firm or a call center.

ENT-11.High startup costs: Some industries need a large investment in buildings, equipment or inventory before the first sale, which many newcomers cannot raise.
ENT-11.Established competitors: Firms already in the market have customers, experience and resources, and a crowded market leaves little room for one more seller.
ENT-11.Government regulation: Licenses, permits, zoning rules and safety or industry regulations can make it slow and costly, or even impossible, for a new firm to enter.
ENT-11.Brand loyalty: Customers who trust and habitually buy existing brands are hard to win over, so a newcomer must spend heavily to get noticed.
ENT-11.Economies of scale: Large established firms produce at a lower cost per unit, so a small new entrant cannot match their prices at first.
ENT-11.Intellectual property: Patents, copyrights and trademarks give their owners exclusive legal rights, so a newcomer cannot legally copy a protected product, process or brand name.
ENT-11.Access to distribution channels: Existing firms already hold the shelf space and the relationships with wholesalers and retailers that a newcomer needs to reach customers.
ENT-11.Switching costs: The money, time or effort a customer must spend to change suppliers. When these are high, customers stay with the firm they already use.
ENT-11.Control of resources: If existing firms own or have tied up a key raw material or supplier, a new business may be unable to get what it needs.
ENT-11.Technology and know-how: Some markets demand specialized technology, skills or knowledge that take years and a lot of money to develop.
ENT-11.Network effects: A product becomes more valuable as more people use it, as with a social network, so users have little reason to join a new, empty rival.
ENT-11.Retaliation by incumbents: Existing firms may respond to a newcomer by cutting prices sharply or boosting promotion, making entry unprofitable.
ENT-11.Exclusive contracts: Agreements that tie suppliers, distributors or customers to existing firms and shut a new business out.
ENT-11.Trade barriers: Tariffs, which are taxes on imported goods, and quotas, which limit how much may be imported, make it harder for a foreign company to enter a market.
ENT-11.High advertising costs: Where established firms advertise heavily, a newcomer must spend large sums on promotion just to be heard.
ENT-11.Government-granted monopoly: The government gives one firm the exclusive right to serve a market, as with many local utilities, so others are not allowed to enter.
ENT-11.Experience curve: Firms that have made a product for years have learned to do it more cheaply and with fewer mistakes than a beginner can.
ENT-11.Lack of good locations: The best sites, such as busy corners or spots near suppliers, may already be taken by existing businesses.

SUP-09.Prices: What each competitor charges, including discounts and price ranges. This shows whether the new business can match, undercut or justify charging more.
SUP-09.Products and services: What each competitor sells, including its range and features, so the new business can see how its own offering compares.
SUP-09.Strengths: The things a competitor does well, such as a loyal following or low costs. These are the areas where it will be hardest to beat.
SUP-09.Weaknesses: The things a competitor does poorly, such as slow service or a narrow selection. Each one is a possible opening for the new business.
SUP-09.Location: Where competitors operate and how many sites they have, which shows which areas are crowded and which are underserved.
SUP-09.Market share: The percentage of total sales in the market that each competitor holds, which shows who the leaders are.
SUP-09.Marketing and promotion: How competitors advertise and promote themselves, including their messages, media and social media activity.
SUP-09.Target customers: The groups of customers each competitor aims at, which reveals segments that nobody is serving well.
SUP-09.Reputation: What customers think and say about a competitor, found in reviews, ratings and word of mouth.
SUP-09.Number of competitors: How many rivals there are and who they are, both direct ones selling the same thing and indirect ones meeting the same need differently.
SUP-09.Sales and revenue: How much a competitor sells and earns, a sign of its size, its financial strength and the demand in the market.
SUP-09.Customer service: How well a competitor treats customers, including its speed, helpfulness, guarantees and return policy.
SUP-09.Quality: How good a competitor's products or services are compared with others in the market.
SUP-09.Distribution channels: The ways a competitor gets its products to customers, such as its own stores, other retailers, a website or delivery.
SUP-09.Size: How large a competitor is in employees and resources, which indicates how strongly it can react to a new rival.
SUP-09.Business strategy: A competitor's goals and plans, such as expanding, cutting prices or moving upmarket, which hint at what it will do next.
SUP-09.Hours of operation: When competitors are open. Longer or different hours can be a simple way for a new business to stand out.
SUP-09.Website and online presence: How easy a competitor is to find and buy from online, including its website and how it shows up in search results.
SUP-09.Unique selling proposition: The main reason a competitor gives customers to choose it over others, which the new business must differ from.
SUP-09.Suppliers: The vendors a competitor buys from, which affects its costs, quality and reliability.
SUP-09.Technology: The equipment, software and production methods a competitor uses, which affect its speed, costs and quality.
SUP-09.Years in business: How long a competitor has been operating. A long history usually means loyal customers and deep experience.

SUP-10.Easy to remember: A name that sticks in people's minds makes it easier for customers to come back and to recommend the business to others.
SUP-10.Name availability: The owner checks that no other business in the state has already registered the same name, usually by searching the state's business records.
SUP-10.Trademark availability: The owner searches trademark records to make sure the name does not copy a protected brand, which could lead to a lawsuit and a forced rename.
SUP-10.Distinctive: A name that is clearly different from competitors' names avoids confusion and is easier to protect as a trademark than a generic one.
SUP-10.Domain name availability: The owner checks whether a matching website address can be registered, since customers expect to find the business online under its name.
SUP-10.Easy to spell: If customers cannot spell the name, they will struggle to search for it online or type its web address.
SUP-10.Describes the business: A name that hints at what the business sells or does helps new customers understand it right away.
SUP-10.Easy to pronounce: A name people can say without hesitating is easier to pass along by word of mouth and to use on the phone or radio.
SUP-10.Short: A brief, simple name is easier to remember and fits better on signs, packaging, web addresses and social media.
SUP-10.Appeals to the target market: The name should suit the tastes and expectations of the customers the business most wants to attract.
SUP-10.Room to grow: A name tied to one product or one town can hold a business back if it later adds products or opens in other places.
SUP-10.Social media handles: The owner checks whether matching usernames are free on the main social media platforms, so customers can find the business easily.
SUP-10.Positive connotations: The feelings and ideas a name brings to mind should be pleasant, with no rude, unlucky or embarrassing second meaning.
SUP-10.Fits the brand image: The name should match the personality the business wants to project, such as playful, luxurious or trustworthy.
SUP-10.Meaning in other languages: A name can mean something odd or offensive in another language, which matters if the business serves diverse or foreign customers.
SUP-10.State naming rules: States set rules for business names, such as requiring a corporation or limited liability company (LLC) to include an ending like Inc. or LLC and restricting certain words.
SUP-10.Works in a logo: The name should look good in print, on a sign and in a logo, since customers will often see it before they hear it.
SUP-10.DBA registration: If the business will trade under a name other than its owner's legal name, it usually must register a "doing business as" (DBA) name.
SUP-10.Timelessness: A name built on a passing fad or slang can sound dated in a few years, so owners look for one that will last.
SUP-10.Search engine friendliness: A name that is easy to find in online search results, and is not buried under other meanings of the same words, brings in more customers.

SUP-11.Rent: The base amount the tenant pays the landlord, usually each month. Commercial rent is often quoted as a price per square foot per year.
SUP-11.Length of the lease: How many years the lease runs. A long term locks in the location and the rent, but also commits a new business to payments for years.
SUP-11.Security deposit: Money the tenant pays up front that the landlord holds in case of unpaid rent or damage to the space.
SUP-11.Utilities: The lease states whether the tenant or the landlord pays for electricity, water, heating, cooling and similar services.
SUP-11.Repairs and maintenance: The lease spells out who must fix and maintain items such as the roof, plumbing, heating and air conditioning. In commercial leases it is often the tenant.
SUP-11.Renewal option: A right for the tenant to extend the lease when it ends, ideally on terms set in advance, so the business cannot simply be forced out.
SUP-11.Rent increases: Many leases include an escalation clause that raises the rent on a schedule or in line with inflation, so the first year's rent is not the final cost.
SUP-11.Termination clause: The conditions under which either side can end the lease early, and what penalties the tenant would owe for doing so.
SUP-11.Square footage: The size of the space being rented. The tenant should check how it is measured, because rent is usually charged per square foot.
SUP-11.Common area maintenance fees: Charges on top of rent for the upkeep of shared areas such as parking lots, hallways, landscaping and lobbies.
SUP-11.Permitted use: The clause that states what kind of business may operate in the space. The planned activities must fit it and local zoning rules.
SUP-11.Subleasing rights: Whether the tenant may rent the space to someone else or transfer the lease, which matters if the business moves, sells or closes.
SUP-11.Leasehold improvements: Changes made to fit the space to the business, such as walls, counters or lighting. The lease says who pays for them and who owns them afterward.
SUP-11.Insurance requirements: The types and amounts of insurance the lease requires the tenant to carry, such as liability coverage.
SUP-11.Property taxes: In some leases the tenant pays all or part of the real estate taxes on the building, on top of the rent.
SUP-11.Type of lease: In a gross lease the landlord covers most building expenses out of the rent. In a net lease the tenant pays some or all of the taxes, insurance and maintenance.
SUP-11.Parking: How many parking spaces customers and employees may use, and whether any are reserved for the business.
SUP-11.Signage rights: What signs the tenant may put up, and where and how large, which affects how easily customers can find the business.
SUP-11.Personal guarantee: A promise by the owner to pay the rent personally if the business cannot, which puts the owner's own assets at risk.
SUP-11.Percentage rent: A clause, common in shopping centers, under which the tenant pays the landlord a share of its sales above a set level in addition to base rent.
SUP-11.Exclusivity clause: A promise by the landlord not to rent other space in the same center to a directly competing business.
SUP-11.Default provisions: The part of the lease that says what counts as breaking it, such as late rent, and what the landlord may do in response.

FND-08.Kickstarter: A rewards-based platform for creative projects and new products. A campaign collects the pledged money only if it reaches its funding goal.
FND-08.GoFundMe: A donation-based platform used mostly for personal needs, emergencies and charitable causes. Donors receive nothing in return.
FND-08.Indiegogo: A rewards-based platform popular for technology and design products, where backers pledge money in exchange for perks or the product itself.
FND-08.Rewards-based crowdfunding: Backers pledge money and in return receive the product or another perk, not ownership. It works like selling a product before it is made.
FND-08.Donation-based crowdfunding: People give money to a cause, person or project and expect nothing back. It is common for charities and personal emergencies.
FND-08.Equity crowdfunding: Many small investors put money into a company online and receive shares or another ownership stake in return. It is regulated as a sale of securities.
FND-08.Patreon: A membership platform where fans pay creators such as artists, podcasters and writers a recurring amount, usually monthly, to support their work.
FND-08.Debt crowdfunding: Many individuals each lend a small amount to a business or person online and are repaid with interest. It is also called peer-to-peer lending.
FND-08.Kiva: A nonprofit platform where people lend small amounts to entrepreneurs, many of them in low-income communities, and are repaid without earning interest.
FND-08.DonorsChoose: A nonprofit donation platform where teachers post classroom projects and members of the public fund the supplies.
FND-08.Wefunder: A U.S. equity crowdfunding platform that lets ordinary people invest small amounts in startups and small businesses.
FND-08.StartEngine: A U.S. equity crowdfunding platform where the public can buy shares in early-stage companies.
FND-08.Republic: An investment platform that offers the public stakes in startups and other private investments.
FND-08.All-or-nothing funding: A campaign model in which backers are charged, and the creator is paid, only if the funding goal is reached by the deadline.
FND-08.Keep-it-all funding: A campaign model, also called flexible funding, in which the creator keeps whatever is pledged even if the goal is not reached.
FND-08.Crowdcube: An equity crowdfunding platform based in the United Kingdom, where the public invests in growing companies in exchange for shares.
FND-08.Real estate crowdfunding: Many investors pool money online to buy or finance property and share in the rent or profit.
FND-08.Recurring crowdfunding: Supporters pay a regular amount, such as a monthly membership, instead of a single pledge, which gives a creator steady income.

FND-09.Interest cost: The borrower pays the lender interest on top of the amount borrowed, so the loan costs more than the money received.
FND-09.Must be repaid: Borrowed money has to be paid back in full. Money from equity investors does not, because they receive ownership instead.
FND-09.Fixed payments: Loan payments fall due on a set schedule, even in months when sales are slow or the business is losing money.
FND-09.Collateral at risk: Lenders often require assets such as equipment or property as security, and can take them if the loan is not repaid.
FND-09.Strain on cash flow: Regular loan payments use up cash that the business could otherwise spend on inventory, marketing or growth.
FND-09.Personal guarantee: Lenders often make a small business owner promise to repay personally, which puts the owner's home and savings at risk.
FND-09.Risk of bankruptcy: A business that cannot make its loan payments is in default, and its lenders can force it to sell assets or close.
FND-09.Hard to qualify: Lenders want good credit, collateral and a track record, which many new businesses do not yet have.
FND-09.Damage to credit rating: Late or missed payments lower the credit scores of the business and often the owner, making later borrowing harder and costlier.
FND-09.Limits future borrowing: A business that already carries a lot of debt looks riskier, so lenders may refuse to lend it more.
FND-09.Higher financial risk: Using more debt, called leverage, increases the fixed costs a business must cover, so a drop in sales hurts it more.
FND-09.Lower profit: Interest is an expense, so it reduces the net income left for the owners.
FND-09.Loan covenants: Conditions in a loan agreement that restrict the borrower, such as limits on taking more debt or a requirement to keep certain financial ratios.
FND-09.Rising interest rates: On a variable-rate loan, payments go up when market interest rates rise, which makes costs harder to predict.
FND-09.Loan fees: Borrowing often carries charges beyond interest, such as application or origination fees and penalties for paying the loan off early.
FND-09.Repayment starts right away: Payments usually begin soon after the loan is made, often before a new business is earning enough to cover them.
FND-09.No investor expertise: A lender supplies only money. Equity investors such as angels and venture capitalists often add advice, mentoring and contacts.
FND-09.Less attractive to investors: Heavy debt can put off future investors, because lenders must be paid before the owners receive anything.

FND-10.Loss of control: Investors usually get a vote on major decisions, so the founder can no longer run the business entirely as he or she sees fit.
FND-10.Giving up ownership: Every share sold to an investor is a piece of the company the founder no longer owns. The shrinking of the founder's percentage is called dilution.
FND-10.Sharing profits: Investors are entitled to their share of all future profits, for as long as they hold their shares. A lender is owed only the loan and its interest.
FND-10.Pressure to grow fast: Investors such as venture capitalists expect a large return, so they push the business to grow quickly even when the founder would prefer a steadier pace.
FND-10.Conflict with investors: Owners and investors may disagree about strategy, spending or when to sell, and those disputes can slow the business down.
FND-10.Takes a long time: Finding investors, pitching to them and negotiating a deal can take months, which pulls the founder away from running the business.
FND-10.Hard to find investors: Angel investors and venture capitalists fund only a small share of the businesses that approach them, mostly ones that could grow very large.
FND-10.Founder can be replaced: If investors gain enough votes or board seats, they can remove the founder from the top job and bring in a different chief executive.
FND-10.Reporting to investors: Investors expect regular financial reports and updates, and the founder must explain and justify the results to them.
FND-10.Costs more in the long run: If the business succeeds, the share of its value handed to investors is usually worth far more than the interest a loan would have cost.
FND-10.Legal and accounting costs: Selling shares requires lawyers and accountants to draw up and check the agreements, and their fees can be large.
FND-10.Board seats for investors: Large investors often require a seat on the board of directors, which gives them a direct voice in how the company is run.
FND-10.Pressure to exit: Investors get their money back only when the company is sold or goes public, so they may push for that before the founder is ready.
FND-10.Permanent: A loan ends when it is paid off, but an investor remains an owner unless someone buys the shares back, which can be costly or impossible.
FND-10.Disclosure of information: Before investing, outsiders examine the company's finances, customers and plans in detail, so information the founder kept private must be shared.
FND-10.No tax deduction: Interest paid on a loan is generally deductible as a business expense, but dividends paid to shareholders are not.
FND-10.Liquidation preference: A common term in investment deals that pays the investors back first when the company is sold or closed, before the founders receive anything.
FND-10.Securities law compliance: Shares are securities, so selling them is governed by federal and state securities laws that add paperwork, rules and legal risk.
FND-10.Undervaluing the company: A young business is hard to value, so a founder who sells shares early may give up a large stake for much less than it later proves to be worth.

GRO-07.Increase market share: Combining with another firm in the same industry adds its customers and sales, giving the buyer a larger slice of the market at once.
GRO-07.Eliminate a competitor: Buying a rival removes it from the market. Antitrust regulators can block deals that would reduce competition too much.
GRO-07.Faster growth: Acquiring a going business adds sales immediately, which is quicker than growing step by step from within.
GRO-07.Enter new markets: Buying a company that already operates in another region or country gives instant access to its customers, staff and local knowledge.
GRO-07.New products: An acquisition adds the other company's products or services to the buyer's line without the time and risk of developing them.
GRO-07.Economies of scale: A larger combined company can spread fixed costs over more units, buy in bulk and cut duplicated functions, lowering its cost per unit.
GRO-07.Acquire technology: A company may buy another to get its technology, patents or software instead of spending years developing its own.
GRO-07.Diversification: Buying a business in a different industry or product area spreads risk, so a slump in one market hurts the company less.
GRO-07.Increase shareholder value: Managers pursue deals they expect will raise profits and so raise the value of the owners' shares.
GRO-07.Synergy: The expected benefit when two companies are worth more together than apart, for example by sharing customers, technology or costs.
GRO-07.Acquire talent: Sometimes the main prize is the other firm's skilled employees or managers. Buying a company mainly for its staff is called an acquihire.
GRO-07.Control the supply chain: Buying a supplier or a distributor, called vertical integration, gives a company more control over its costs, quality and supply.
GRO-07.Acquire a brand: A well-known brand name takes years to build, so a company may buy the business that owns it.
GRO-07.Distribution channels: An acquisition can bring the other company's dealers, stores or sales force, opening new ways to reach customers.
GRO-07.Tax benefits: In some cases a deal lowers the combined company's tax bill, for example by using the past losses of one firm against the profits of the other.
GRO-07.Undervalued target: A buyer may believe the other company can be bought for less than it is really worth, making the purchase a bargain.
GRO-07.Stronger bargaining power: A bigger company buys more, so it can negotiate better prices and terms from suppliers and sometimes from customers.
GRO-07.Access to capital: A merger can give a company the cash or borrowing strength of its partner to fund projects it could not afford alone.
GRO-07.Survival: A struggling company may agree to merge or be bought because it cannot keep going alone.
GRO-07.Acquire production capacity: Buying a company with factories, equipment or stores already in place is faster than building new facilities.

GRO-08.Merger: Two companies agree to join together and carry on as one company.
GRO-08.Acquisition: One company buys another, or enough of its shares to control it, and takes charge of its operations.
GRO-08.Horizontal merger: A combination of two companies that sell the same kind of product in the same market, such as two grocery chains. It removes a competitor.
GRO-08.Vertical merger: A combination of companies at different stages of the same supply chain, such as a furniture maker buying a lumber mill or a chain of furniture stores.
GRO-08.Hostile takeover: An acquisition carried out against the wishes of the target company's managers, usually by offering to buy shares directly from its shareholders.
GRO-08.Conglomerate merger: A combination of companies in unrelated industries, such as a food maker and an insurance firm, usually done to spread risk.
GRO-08.Joint venture: Two or more companies set up a separate business together for a shared project and split its costs, control and profits. Each parent stays independent.
GRO-08.Leveraged buyout: The purchase of a company paid for mostly with borrowed money, which is then repaid out of the purchased company's own cash flow.
GRO-08.Friendly takeover: An acquisition that the managers and board of the target company agree to and recommend to their shareholders.
GRO-08.Management buyout: The managers who already run a company, or one of its divisions, buy it from its current owners.
GRO-08.Consolidation: Two or more companies combine to form an entirely new company, and the original companies no longer exist.
GRO-08.Reverse merger: A private company becomes publicly traded by merging with a company that is already listed on a stock exchange, instead of holding its own stock offering.
GRO-08.Tender offer: A public offer made directly to a company's shareholders to buy their shares at a stated price, usually above the market price.
GRO-08.Market extension merger: A combination of companies that sell the same products in different geographic areas, giving each access to the other's territory.
GRO-08.Product extension merger: A combination of companies that sell different but related products in the same market, such as a soft drink maker and a snack maker.
GRO-08.Asset purchase: The buyer acquires chosen assets of a business, such as its equipment, inventory and brand names, instead of buying the company itself.
GRO-08.Stock purchase: The buyer acquires the owners' shares, and so takes over the whole company along with all of its assets, contracts and debts.
GRO-08.Roll-up: A buyer acquires many small companies in the same industry and joins them into one larger company.
GRO-08.Acquihire: A company is bought mainly to gain its skilled employees, not its products or customers.
GRO-08.Bolt-on acquisition: A larger company buys a smaller one in the same line of business and folds it into an existing division.
GRO-08.Special purpose acquisition company: A company with no business of its own that raises money from the public and then merges with a private company to take it public. It is known as a SPAC.

GRO-09.Cut costs: The business reduces spending on everything that is not essential, so that less cash goes out each month.
GRO-09.Lay off employees: Payroll is often the largest expense, so a struggling business may reduce its staff to match its lower sales.
GRO-09.Close unprofitable locations: Shutting stores, branches or plants that lose money stops those losses and lets the business concentrate on sites that earn a profit.
GRO-09.Sell assets: Selling a division, a building or unused equipment brings in cash quickly to pay debts and fund what remains.
GRO-09.Increase marketing: New advertising and promotions aim to win back customers and lift sales, which is necessary if falling revenue is the problem.
GRO-09.Raise prices: If prices are too low to cover costs, raising them improves the profit on each sale, provided customers do not leave.
GRO-09.Drop unprofitable products: Removing products that lose money or sell poorly frees cash, shelf space and attention for the items that do earn a profit.
GRO-09.Renegotiate debt: The business asks lenders and other creditors for easier terms, such as lower payments, a longer time to pay or a reduced balance.
GRO-09.Raise new capital: Fresh money from investors or lenders gives the business time and resources to carry out its recovery plan.
GRO-09.Chapter 11 bankruptcy: A court-supervised process that protects a business from creditors while it keeps operating and works out a plan to repay its debts.
GRO-09.Replace management: Owners or the board bring in new leaders, sometimes turnaround specialists, when the current managers caused or cannot fix the problems.
GRO-09.Rebrand: The business changes its name, look or image to shed a poor reputation and appeal to customers again.
GRO-09.Pivot: The business changes its strategy or business model, for example by serving a different customer or selling in a different way.
GRO-09.Launch new products: Fresh or updated products can replace ones that customers have stopped buying and bring sales back.
GRO-09.Improve quality or service: If customers left because of poor products or poor treatment, fixing those problems is the way to win them back.
GRO-09.Focus on the core business: The business drops side activities and puts its limited money and effort into the products and customers it serves best.
GRO-09.Renegotiate leases and contracts: The business asks landlords and suppliers for lower rent, better prices or longer payment terms to reduce what it pays out.
GRO-09.Improve cash collection: Collecting money that customers owe more quickly brings in cash without needing new sales.
GRO-09.Reduce inventory: Selling off excess stock, even at a discount, turns goods sitting on shelves into cash and lowers storage costs.
GRO-09.Outsource: Paying an outside company to do a task, such as payroll or delivery, can cost less than keeping staff and equipment for it.
GRO-09.Refinance: The business replaces existing loans with a new one that has a lower interest rate or a longer term, reducing its monthly payments.
GRO-09.Pay cuts: Owners, executives or staff accept lower pay or unpaid time off for a while, which saves cash and can avoid some layoffs.
GRO-09.Merge with a stronger company: Joining or being bought by a healthier company can supply the money and management a struggling business lacks.
GRO-09.Cut dividends: A corporation stops or reduces the payments it makes to shareholders so that it can keep the cash in the business.

GRO-10.Economies of scale: As a business produces more, its fixed costs are spread over more units, so the cost of making each unit falls.
GRO-10.Brand recognition: Customers already know and trust a large company's name, so it has to do less to persuade them to buy.
GRO-10.More financial resources: A large business has more cash and assets to invest in equipment, stores, staff and new projects.
GRO-10.Bulk buying discounts: Suppliers give lower prices per unit to customers that order in large quantities, so a big business pays less for what it buys.
GRO-10.Easier access to financing: Lenders see large, established companies as safer, so they lend to them more readily and at lower rates. Large corporations can also sell stock and bonds.
GRO-10.Lower prices: Because its costs per unit are lower, a large business can charge customers less than a small rival and still make a profit.
GRO-10.Larger advertising budget: A big company can afford national campaigns, and the cost is spread over many sales, so advertising costs less per unit sold.
GRO-10.Specialized employees: A large firm can hire experts for each job, such as accountants, lawyers and marketers, where a small owner must do many jobs personally.
GRO-10.Attracts talent: Large companies can usually offer higher pay, better benefits and more chances for promotion, which helps them hire skilled people.
GRO-10.Wider product range: A large business can stock or produce many more products, giving customers more choice in one place.
GRO-10.Research and development: Large firms can afford laboratories and staff to develop new products and improve old ones, which is too costly for most small firms.
GRO-10.Diversification: A big company that sells many products in many markets is hurt less when one of them does badly.
GRO-10.Wider geographic reach: With many locations, a large business can serve customers across a country or around the world.
GRO-10.Market power: A firm with a large share of the market has more influence over prices, suppliers and retailers than a small competitor.
GRO-10.Better technology: Large companies can afford advanced equipment, software and automation that make them faster and more efficient.
GRO-10.Survive downturns: With cash reserves and several sources of income, a big business can absorb losses in a bad year that would close a small one.
GRO-10.Distribution network: Many large firms run their own warehouses and trucks or have strong ties with distributors, so goods reach customers cheaply and reliably.
GRO-10.Experience and systems: An established large business has tested procedures and years of know-how, so it makes fewer costly mistakes.
GRO-10.Political influence: Large companies can afford lobbyists and trade groups to argue their case to lawmakers and regulators.
GRO-10.Legal resources: A big business can keep lawyers on staff to handle contracts, regulations and lawsuits that would overwhelm a small firm.

INO-08.No market need: The product does not solve a problem that enough people care about, so few customers want to buy it.
INO-08.Priced too high: Customers do not think the product is worth what it costs, especially when cheaper alternatives exist.
INO-08.Poor quality: The product breaks, performs badly or does not do what it claims, so buyers return it and warn others away.
INO-08.Poor marketing: Too few people in the target market hear about the product or understand why they should want it.
INO-08.Strong competition: Rivals already offer something as good or better, or they respond to the launch with price cuts and new products of their own.
INO-08.Poor timing: The product arrives too early, before customers are ready for it, or too late, after competitors have won the market.
INO-08.Insufficient market research: The company did not study or test what customers want before launching, so it built the product on wrong assumptions.
INO-08.Not different enough: The product offers nothing clearly better or new, so customers see no reason to switch from what they already use.
INO-08.Poor design: The product is confusing, awkward or unattractive, which puts customers off even if the idea behind it is good.
INO-08.Overestimated market size: The company expected far more buyers than really exist, so sales never reach the level needed to make a profit.
INO-08.Poor positioning: The product is aimed at the wrong customers or presented with an unclear message, so the people who might buy it do not notice it.
INO-08.Distribution problems: The product is hard to find because too few stores or channels carry it, so interested customers cannot buy it.
INO-08.High development costs: Designing and making the product costs more than planned, so it cannot be sold at a price that earns a profit.
INO-08.Changing consumer tastes: Customer preferences or trends shift between the time the product was planned and the time it reaches the market.
INO-08.Production problems: The company cannot make enough units, or make them on time, so shelves are empty when customers want to buy.
INO-08.Safety or legal problems: The product turns out to be unsafe or to break a regulation, leading to recalls, lawsuits or a ban.
INO-08.Poor customer support: Buyers who need help, repairs or instructions cannot get them, which leads to bad reviews and returns.
INO-08.Fails to meet expectations: Advertising promised more than the product delivers, so disappointed buyers do not come back or recommend it.
INO-08.Economic downturn: In a weak economy consumers cut back on spending and are less willing to try something new.
INO-08.Cannibalization: The new product mostly takes sales away from the company's own existing products instead of adding new sales.
INO-08.Lack of company support: The company does not commit enough money, staff or management attention to launch the product properly.

INO-09.Rewards and bonuses: The company pays cash, prizes or other incentives to employees whose ideas are adopted, giving people a reason to speak up.
INO-09.Brainstorming sessions: Group meetings held to produce as many ideas as possible, with criticism saved for later so people feel free to contribute.
INO-09.Suggestion box: A system, physical or online, where any employee can submit ideas for new products or better ways of working.
INO-09.Research and development budget: Money set aside for research and development (R&D), so employees have the funds and equipment to explore and test new ideas.
INO-09.Training: Courses and workshops that teach creative thinking, problem solving and new skills that employees can apply to their work.
INO-09.Recognition: Publicly praising or giving awards to people who come up with good ideas shows that the company values innovation.
INO-09.Time for side projects: Some companies let employees spend part of their paid working hours on projects of their own choosing that might benefit the business.
INO-09.Hackathons: Short, intense events, often a day or two, in which teams of employees race to build and present a new idea or prototype.
INO-09.Tolerating failure: Managers accept that some experiments will not work and do not punish honest failed attempts, so employees dare to try new things.
INO-09.Open communication: Managers invite ideas from every level and listen to them, so a good suggestion can come from anyone in the company.
INO-09.Intrapreneurship programs: Programs that let employees develop a new product or venture inside the company, acting like entrepreneurs with the company's backing.
INO-09.Cross-functional teams: Teams that bring together people from different departments, such as engineering, marketing and finance, whose mixed viewpoints spark new ideas.
INO-09.Autonomy: Giving employees the freedom to decide how to do their work and to act on their ideas without waiting for approval at every step.
INO-09.Leadership support: Top managers visibly back new ideas with their time, attention and resources, which signals that innovation matters.
INO-09.Innovation labs: Separate teams or spaces, sometimes called skunkworks, where staff develop new ideas away from daily routines and normal company rules.
INO-09.Diverse hiring: Employing people with different backgrounds, skills and experiences brings a wider range of viewpoints and ideas.
INO-09.Creative workspaces: Offices designed with shared areas, whiteboards and informal meeting spots to make it easy for people to meet and swap ideas.
INO-09.Flat structure: An organization with few layers of management, so ideas reach decision makers quickly instead of being lost on the way up.
INO-09.Employee ownership: Stock options or profit sharing give employees a share in the company's success, so they gain personally when their ideas pay off.
INO-09.Job rotation: Moving employees through different jobs or departments gives them new knowledge and a fresh view of how things could be improved.
INO-09.Innovation goals: Setting targets, such as a share of sales that must come from new products, and judging managers on them makes innovation part of the job.

INO-10.Lack of funding: Developing and testing new ideas costs money, and a company that will not or cannot budget for it gets few of them.
INO-10.Fear of failure: When mistakes are punished, employees and managers avoid risky new ideas and stick to what is safe.
INO-10.Resistance to change: People are comfortable with familiar ways of working and may oppose new ideas that disrupt their routines or threaten their roles.
INO-10.Lack of time: Employees who are fully occupied with daily tasks and deadlines have no time left to think about or try anything new.
INO-10.Bureaucracy: Rigid rules, many layers of management and slow approvals delay or kill ideas before they can be tested.
INO-10.Short-term focus: Pressure to hit this quarter's profit targets leads managers to cut projects that will only pay off years later.
INO-10.Lack of leadership support: If top managers do not back innovation with attention and resources, new ideas rarely get beyond the proposal stage.
INO-10.Poor communication: Ideas go nowhere when employees have no way to share them or when managers do not listen.
INO-10.Silos: Departments that do not share information or work together miss the combinations of knowledge that produce new ideas.
INO-10.Lack of skills: The company's employees may not have the technical knowledge, creativity training or experience needed to develop something new.
INO-10.No incentives: If good ideas bring no reward or recognition, employees have little reason to make the extra effort.
INO-10.Complacency: A company that has been successful may believe it does not need to change, and so ignores new ideas until rivals overtake it.
INO-10.Outdated technology: Old equipment and computer systems can make it difficult or expensive to add new products and processes.
INO-10.Groupthink: Members of a close group go along with the majority to keep harmony, so unusual ideas and doubts are never voiced.
INO-10.Lack of customer insight: A company that does not study what customers really need cannot tell which new ideas are worth pursuing.
INO-10.No clear innovation strategy: Without stated goals and a process for collecting, choosing and funding ideas, innovation happens only by accident.
INO-10.Not-invented-here syndrome: The tendency of people in a company to reject ideas and technology that come from outside, simply because they did not create them.
INO-10.Fear of cannibalizing existing products: A company may hold back a new product because it would take sales from the profitable products it already sells.
INO-10.Micromanagement: Managers who control every detail leave employees no freedom to experiment or to act on their own ideas.

INO-11.Aging population: People are living longer and older adults make up a growing share of the population, raising demand for home care, health services and senior housing.
INO-11.Health and wellness: More consumers want to eat well, exercise and look after their mental health, which opens markets for gyms, healthy food and wellness services.
INO-11.Sustainability: Growing concern for the environment leads consumers to seek products that create less waste and pollution, such as reusable goods and clean energy.
INO-11.Remote work: Many people now work from home at least part of the week, creating demand for home office goods, collaboration tools and services near where they live.
INO-11.Online shopping: Consumers buy more and more over the internet, so a small business can reach customers anywhere without opening a physical store.
INO-11.Social media use: People spend hours a day on social platforms, creating opportunities in content creation, influencer marketing and selling directly to followers.
INO-11.Gig economy: More people earn income from short-term, freelance or app-based jobs, which creates demand for platforms and services that support independent workers.
INO-11.Demand for convenience: Busy consumers will pay to save time, which drives businesses such as meal delivery, on-demand services and one-click ordering.
INO-11.Pet ownership: Many owners treat pets as family members and spend more on them, supporting businesses in premium pet food, grooming, daycare and pet health.
INO-11.Plant-based eating: More consumers are cutting back on meat and dairy for health, ethical or environmental reasons, creating demand for alternative foods.
INO-11.Growing diversity: As the population becomes more varied in ethnicity and culture, demand rises for foods, media, beauty products and services that fit different groups.
INO-11.Urbanization: More people live in cities, where small living spaces and dense neighborhoods favor businesses such as delivery, shared transport and compact housing.
INO-11.Buying local: Many consumers prefer to support nearby producers and independent shops, which helps farmers markets, craft makers and local restaurants.
INO-11.Sharing economy: People increasingly rent or share things such as rides, rooms and tools through online platforms instead of owning them.
INO-11.Secondhand shopping: Buying used clothing, furniture and electronics has become more popular, driven by lower prices and concern about waste.
INO-11.Experiences over things: Many consumers, especially younger ones, would sooner spend on travel, events and activities than on possessions.
INO-11.Personalization: Customers increasingly expect products and services tailored to their own tastes, sizes or needs instead of one standard version.
INO-11.Subscription services: Consumers have grown used to paying a regular fee for ongoing access or deliveries, from streaming video to meal kits.
INO-11.Dual-income households: In many families both adults work, leaving less time for chores and raising demand for child care, cleaning and prepared meals.
INO-11.Lifelong learning: Adults keep studying to change careers or update their skills, creating demand for online courses, tutoring and training.
INO-11.Smaller households: More people live alone or have fewer children, which raises demand for smaller homes, single-serving products and social activities.
INO-11.Cashless payments: Shoppers increasingly pay with cards and phones instead of cash, creating openings for payment services and making online selling easier.
INO-11.Ethical consumerism: A growing number of buyers choose brands based on how they treat workers, animals and communities, not only on price.
INO-11.Minimalism: Some consumers deliberately own fewer things, favoring quality over quantity and services such as rental, repair and organizing.
INO-11.Do-it-yourself culture: Many people enjoy making, repairing and improving things themselves, which supports craft supplies, tools, kits and how-to content.

SBM-09.Social media: Posting photos, videos and news on platforms such as Instagram, Facebook or TikTok costs nothing but time and reaches local followers directly.
SBM-09.Word of mouth: Satisfied customers telling friends and family about the business. It is free and trusted more than advertising.
SBM-09.Referral program: The business rewards existing customers, for example with a discount, when they bring in a new customer.
SBM-09.Website: A simple site showing what the business sells, where it is and how to contact it lets customers find it at any hour for a small yearly cost.
SBM-09.Email marketing: Sending news and offers to customers who have given their email address. It costs very little per message and reaches people who already like the business.
SBM-09.Flyers: Printed sheets handed out, posted on notice boards or left on doorsteps to announce the business or an offer to people nearby.
SBM-09.Coupons: Offers of a lower price or a free extra that give new customers a reason to try the business and existing ones a reason to return.
SBM-09.Business cards: Small printed cards with the business name and contact details that the owner hands to everyone met, at very low cost each.
SBM-09.Online business listing: A free profile on search engines, maps and review sites that shows the business's hours, address and phone number to people searching nearby.
SBM-09.Online reviews: Asking happy customers to post ratings and comments online builds trust with people who are deciding where to buy.
SBM-09.Networking: Meeting other business owners and potential customers through groups such as the local chamber of commerce, which leads to referrals.
SBM-09.Community events: Taking part in or sponsoring local fairs, markets, charity drives and youth teams puts the business name in front of neighbors.
SBM-09.Signage: A clear sign on the building, in the window or on the sidewalk tells everyone passing by that the business exists and what it sells.
SBM-09.Search engine optimization: Improving a website so it appears higher in unpaid search results (SEO), which brings in visitors without paying for ads.
SBM-09.Cross-promotion: Two businesses that serve the same customers but do not compete agree to promote each other, for example by sharing flyers or offers.
SBM-09.Publicity: Unpaid coverage in local news media, often won by sending a press release, a short written announcement of an opening, event or achievement.
SBM-09.Loyalty program: A punch card or points system that rewards repeat purchases, for example with a free item after a set number of visits.
SBM-09.Free samples: Letting people try a small amount of the product at no charge, so they can judge it for themselves before buying.
SBM-09.Content marketing: Publishing useful or entertaining articles, videos or podcasts related to the business, which attracts customers and shows expertise.
SBM-09.Guerrilla marketing: Unusual, creative, low-budget tactics in public places that surprise people and get them talking about the business.
SBM-09.Vehicle signage: Putting the business name, logo and phone number on a car or van turns every trip into a moving advertisement.
SBM-09.Direct mail: Postcards or letters sent to homes in a chosen neighborhood, a cheap way to reach every household near the business.
SBM-09.Contests: A prize drawing or competition, often run on social media, that draws attention and collects the names of interested people.
SBM-09.Branded merchandise: Low-cost items such as stickers, pens or T-shirts printed with the logo, which keep the business name in view.
SBM-09.Local influencers: People with a modest but loyal local following online who mention the business, often in exchange for free products instead of large fees.
SBM-09.User-generated content: Photos, videos and posts made by customers themselves, which the business encourages and shares as free and believable promotion.
SBM-09.Free workshops: The owner teaches a free class or gives a talk on a related subject, which shows expertise and brings likely customers through the door.
SBM-09.Online community groups: Taking part helpfully in neighborhood apps and local social media groups, where residents ask for and give recommendations.
SBM-09.Text message marketing: Sending short offers and reminders by text to customers who have agreed to receive them. Texts are cheap and almost always read.

SBM-10.Income tax: A tax on the profit a business earns, charged by the federal government and most states. In a sole proprietorship, partnership or most limited liability companies, the owners pay it on their personal returns.
SBM-10.Sales tax: A tax on retail sales set by states and localities. The business adds it to the customer's bill, collects it and sends it to the government.
SBM-10.Payroll tax: Taxes on the wages a business pays, mainly Social Security and Medicare, together known as FICA. The employer pays one share and withholds the employee's share from each paycheck.
SBM-10.Property tax: A local tax on the value of land and buildings a business owns. Many places also tax business equipment.
SBM-10.Self-employment tax: The Social Security and Medicare tax paid by people who work for themselves. They pay both the employee and the employer shares.
SBM-10.Corporate income tax: A tax on the profits of a corporation, paid by the corporation itself before any profit is passed to shareholders.
SBM-10.Unemployment tax: Federal and state taxes paid by employers to fund benefits for workers who lose their jobs.
SBM-10.Excise tax: A tax on specific goods or activities, such as fuel, tobacco, alcohol and air travel, usually included in the price.
SBM-10.Income tax withholding: An employer must take income tax out of each employee's paycheck and send it to the government on the employee's behalf.
SBM-10.Estimated tax: Owners with no employer withholding their tax must pay their expected income and self-employment tax in installments through the year.
SBM-10.Use tax: A tax a business owes its state on items bought without paying sales tax, for example from an out-of-state seller, and then used in the state.
SBM-10.Franchise tax: A tax some states charge a business for the right to exist or operate in the state. It has nothing to do with franchising.
SBM-10.Tariffs: Taxes charged on goods brought into a country. A business that imports products or materials pays them at the border.
SBM-10.Local business tax: Some cities and counties charge businesses a tax for operating there, often tied to a business license.
SBM-10.Capital gains tax: A tax on the profit made when an asset such as property, equipment or the business itself is sold for more than it cost.
SBM-10.Gross receipts tax: A tax some states and cities charge on a business's total revenue, with no subtraction for its costs.
SBM-10.Lodging tax: A tax that hotels, inns and short-term rentals collect from guests on the room price and pass on to the state or city.
SBM-10.Value-added tax: A tax on the value added at each stage of production, used in many countries outside the United States. A firm that sells there may have to collect it.

SBM-11.Dress code: The rules on what employees may wear at work, including any uniform and standards for grooming and personal appearance.
SBM-11.Attendance: The rules on showing up for work on time, how to report an absence and what happens when someone is repeatedly late or absent.
SBM-11.Paid time off: How many paid vacation days and holidays employees receive, how the days are earned and how to request them.
SBM-11.Code of conduct: The standards of behavior and ethics the business expects from employees toward customers, coworkers and the company.
SBM-11.Anti-harassment policy: A statement that harassment, including sexual harassment, is not tolerated, with instructions for reporting it and a promise to investigate.
SBM-11.Sick leave: The time an employee may take off for illness, whether it is paid and what notice or proof is required.
SBM-11.Pay and payroll: When and how employees are paid, including pay periods, paydays, deductions and how hours are recorded.
SBM-11.Benefits: The extras offered on top of wages, such as health insurance and retirement plans, and who qualifies for them.
SBM-11.Work hours: The normal working hours and schedules, and the rules for meal and rest breaks.
SBM-11.Overtime: Who is eligible for overtime pay, how it is calculated and whether a manager must approve extra hours in advance.
SBM-11.Safety: The rules for working safely, what to do in an emergency and how to report an accident or injury.
SBM-11.Equal employment opportunity: A statement that the business does not discriminate in hiring, pay or promotion on grounds such as race, sex, religion, age or disability.
SBM-11.Disciplinary procedures: The steps the business takes when rules are broken, often moving from a spoken warning to a written warning and then to dismissal.
SBM-11.Social media policy: The rules on what employees may post online about the company, its customers and their coworkers.
SBM-11.Technology use: The rules for using company computers, email and internet access, usually with notice that the company may monitor them.
SBM-11.Cell phone policy: The rules on when employees may use personal phones during working hours.
SBM-11.Drug and alcohol policy: A ban on working under the influence of drugs or alcohol, often with the conditions under which employees may be tested.
SBM-11.Confidentiality: The duty of employees to keep customer data, trade secrets and other private company information from being shared outside the business.
SBM-11.Termination: How employment ends, including the notice asked of employees who resign, return of company property and the final paycheck.
SBM-11.Leave of absence: The longer kinds of time off an employee may take, such as family and medical leave, parental leave, bereavement leave and jury duty.
SBM-11.At-will employment: A statement that either the employer or the employee may end the job at any time, for any lawful reason, and that the handbook is not a contract.
SBM-11.Performance reviews: How and when an employee's work is evaluated, and how the results affect raises and promotions.
SBM-11.Conflict of interest: Rules that stop employees from letting personal interests clash with the company's, covering matters like gifts from suppliers and second jobs.
SBM-11.Complaint procedure: The steps an employee should follow to raise a problem or grievance, and whom to tell, without fear of punishment.
SBM-11.Company mission and values: An opening section that welcomes the employee and explains what the business stands for, its history and its goals.
SBM-11.Remote work policy: The rules on who may work from home, when, and what is expected of them in hours, equipment and communication.
SBM-11.Expense reimbursement: How employees are paid back for approved costs of doing their job, such as travel and mileage, and what receipts they must provide.
SBM-11.Acknowledgment form: A page the employee signs to confirm having received and read the handbook. The business keeps it on file.
SBM-11.Employee classifications: Definitions of the categories of employee, such as full-time and part-time, and exempt or nonexempt from overtime, which decide pay rules and benefits.
SBM-11.Workplace violence: A ban on threats, fighting and, usually, weapons at work, with instructions for reporting anything that seems dangerous.

FRN-09.Unlimited liability: The owner is personally responsible for every debt and lawsuit of the business, so a home, car and savings can be taken to pay them.
FRN-09.Limited capital: The business has only the owner's own money and whatever the owner can borrow personally, which is usually far less than partners or shareholders could supply.
FRN-09.Limited life: The business has no legal existence apart from its owner, so it ends when the owner dies, retires or quits unless it is sold or handed on.
FRN-09.Heavy workload: With no co-owners to share the work, the proprietor often puts in long hours and finds it hard to take a day off.
FRN-09.All the responsibility: Every decision and every problem lands on one person, with no co-owner to share the burden.
FRN-09.Limited skills: One person is rarely good at everything a business needs, such as selling, accounting, managing staff and marketing.
FRN-09.Bears all losses: Just as the owner keeps all the profit, the owner alone absorbs every loss the business makes.
FRN-09.Stress: Carrying all the risk, work and decisions alone puts constant pressure on a sole proprietor.
FRN-09.No one to share ideas with: A sole owner has no partner to discuss decisions with, to offer a second opinion or to share the load.
FRN-09.Difficulty hiring employees: Talented workers often prefer larger firms that can offer higher pay, better benefits and more room for promotion.
FRN-09.Limited growth: With limited money, time and management skill, a business owned by one person finds it hard to expand.
FRN-09.Unstable income: The owner's pay is whatever profit is left, so it rises and falls with sales and is never guaranteed.
FRN-09.Self-employment tax: A sole proprietor pays both the employee share and the employer share of Social Security and Medicare taxes on the business's profit.
FRN-09.Few fringe benefits: No employer provides the owner with health insurance, paid vacation or a retirement plan, so the owner must arrange and pay for them.
FRN-09.Difficult to sell or transfer: There are no shares to sell, and the business depends so heavily on its owner that finding a buyer or successor can be hard.
FRN-09.Illness stops the business: If the owner is sick, injured or away, there may be nobody able to keep the business running.
FRN-09.Less credibility: Some lenders, suppliers and large customers see a sole proprietorship as less established than a corporation or limited liability company.
FRN-09.Cannot sell stock: A sole proprietorship has no shares, so the owner cannot raise money by selling part of the ownership to investors without changing the form of business.

FRN-10.Existing customers: The business already has people who buy from it regularly, so the new owner does not have to build a customer base from nothing.
