FRN-10.Established reputation: The business is already known and trusted in its market. The value of that name and those relationships is called goodwill.
FRN-10.Proven track record: Past sales, costs and profits show how the business really performs, so the buyer can judge it on facts instead of guesses.
FRN-10.Immediate cash flow: Sales continue from the first day of ownership, while a brand new business may wait months before money comes in.
FRN-10.Trained employees: Staff who already know the products, customers and routines stay on, which saves the time and cost of hiring and training.
FRN-10.Less risk: A business that has survived and made a profit has already proved there is demand, which makes it a safer bet than an untested idea.
FRN-10.Established location: The site is already set up and its ability to attract customers is known, so the buyer avoids the search for premises.
FRN-10.Equipment in place: The machinery, furniture and fixtures needed to operate are included in the purchase and already installed.
FRN-10.Supplier relationships: The business already has vendors who know it and supply it, often on credit terms a new firm would not get.
FRN-10.Easier financing: Lenders are more willing to finance the purchase of a business with a record of sales and profits than an unproven startup.
FRN-10.Saves time: The buyer skips the months of planning, building, hiring and promotion that it takes to get a new business open.
FRN-10.Inventory in place: The shelves and stockroom are already filled with goods, chosen with knowledge of what customers actually buy.
FRN-10.Systems in place: Procedures for ordering, pricing, record keeping and daily operations have already been worked out and tested.
FRN-10.Established market share: The business already holds a portion of the sales in its market, which a newcomer would have to fight to win.
FRN-10.Seller training: The previous owner often agrees to stay for a period after the sale to teach the buyer how the business runs and introduce key contacts.
FRN-10.Seller financing: The seller may let the buyer pay part of the price over time, which reduces the amount the buyer must borrow from a bank.
FRN-10.Licenses and permits in place: The business already holds approvals it needs to operate, though the buyer must check which ones can be transferred.
FRN-10.Bargain price: An owner who must sell quickly, for example because of retirement or illness, may accept less than the business is worth.
FRN-10.Existing contracts: Agreements with customers or suppliers may pass to the buyer, bringing guaranteed sales or favorable terms.
FRN-10.Removes a competitor: Taking over a business that is already in the market, instead of opening a new one beside it, means not having to compete against it.
FRN-10.Intellectual property included: The purchase can include the business's trade names, trademarks, patents and recipes or designs.

FRN-11.Fast food: Quick-service restaurants are the best-known franchises. A standard menu, kitchen layout and training make each outlet easy to copy.
FRN-11.Hotels: Many hotels that carry a famous brand name are owned by independent franchisees who pay to use the brand and its reservation system.
FRN-11.Fitness centers: Gyms and exercise studios are often franchised, with members drawn by a known brand and a standard set of equipment and classes.
FRN-11.Coffee shops: Coffee and donut shops with a fixed menu and store design are widely franchised.
FRN-11.Auto repair: Oil change, muffler, brake, tire and general repair shops are commonly franchised, since drivers trust a familiar name with their cars.
FRN-11.Specialty retail stores: Some specialty stores, selling goods such as vitamins, batteries or sporting goods, are franchised, with the franchisor supplying the brand, the store design and often the merchandise.
FRN-11.Full-service restaurants: Many casual dining restaurants with table service are franchised as well, though they cost much more to open than a fast food outlet.
FRN-11.Ice cream and frozen desserts: Ice cream, frozen yogurt and smoothie shops are a long-established type of food franchise with small stores and simple menus.
FRN-11.Convenience stores: Small stores open long hours and selling everyday items are often run by franchisees, sometimes together with a gas station.
FRN-11.Hair salons: Walk-in haircut chains and other salons are frequently franchised, with the owner hiring licensed stylists.
FRN-11.Real estate: Many local real estate offices are independently owned franchises operating under a national brand name.
FRN-11.Cleaning services: Home and office cleaning are popular franchises because they need little equipment and no storefront, so they cost less to start.
FRN-11.Car dealerships: A new-car dealer is an independent business with a franchise from a manufacturer to sell and service its vehicles in an area.
FRN-11.Tax preparation: Offices that prepare income tax returns for the public are often franchised, using the franchisor's software, training and brand.
FRN-11.Tutoring: Learning centers that offer tutoring and test preparation to children are a common education franchise.
FRN-11.Child care: Daycare centers and preschools are franchised, with the franchisor providing the curriculum, safety standards and brand.
FRN-11.Senior care: Franchises that send caregivers to help older adults in their homes have grown as the population ages.
FRN-11.Home services: Plumbing, painting, pest control, repair and restoration businesses are often franchised, and many run from a van instead of a shop.
FRN-11.Lawn care: Lawn treatment and landscaping franchises serve homeowners on a regular schedule, often from a truck with no storefront.
FRN-11.Car rental: Many car rental locations, especially outside the big airports, are operated by franchisees under a national brand.
FRN-11.Shipping and printing: Stores that pack and ship parcels, rent mailboxes and print documents or signs are a common business-service franchise.
FRN-11.Pet services: Pet grooming, boarding, daycare and supply stores are a growing franchise category as owners spend more on their animals.
FRN-11.Soft drink bottling: Soft drink companies have long licensed local bottlers to make and distribute their drinks in a set territory, an early form of franchising.
FRN-11.Staffing agencies: Offices that supply temporary and permanent workers to employers are often franchised under national names.
FRN-11.Travel agencies: Some travel agencies, including home-based cruise and vacation planners, operate as franchises of a larger brand.
FRN-11.Health services: Some urgent care clinics, chiropractic offices, physical therapy practices and eyewear stores operate as franchises.
FRN-11.Moving services: Local moving and junk removal companies are often franchises that share a brand, a call center and a booking system.

GRO-11.Get a valuation: The owner works out what the business is worth, often with a professional appraiser, so the asking price is realistic and can be defended.
GRO-11.Find a buyer: The owner or a broker advertises the business and approaches likely buyers, such as competitors, employees, family members or investors.
GRO-11.Negotiate the price: Seller and buyer bargain over the price and the other terms, such as how and when the money will be paid.
GRO-11.Organize financial records: The owner gets several years of financial statements and tax returns accurate and in order, because buyers and their lenders will study them.
GRO-11.Hire a business broker: A broker is a professional who values the business, finds and screens buyers and helps with the negotiation in return for a commission.
GRO-11.Sign a purchase agreement: The final contract that states exactly what is being sold, the price, how it will be paid and what each side promises.
GRO-11.Due diligence: The seller opens the records, contracts and premises to the buyer, who checks that everything said about the business is true.
GRO-11.Hire an attorney: A lawyer writes and reviews the sale documents and makes sure the seller is protected from claims after the sale.
GRO-11.Closing: The meeting or moment when the documents are signed, the money is paid and ownership passes to the buyer.
GRO-11.Improve profitability: In the years before a sale the owner raises sales and trims wasteful costs, because buyers pay more for a business with strong, steady profit.
GRO-11.Confidentiality agreement: Possible buyers sign a promise not to reveal or use what they learn about the business, which protects it if the sale falls through.
GRO-11.Train the new owner: The seller agrees to stay for a set time after the sale to teach the buyer the business and introduce customers and suppliers.
GRO-11.Screen buyers: The seller checks that an interested person is serious and has the money or financing to buy, before sharing private details.
GRO-11.Letter of intent: A short document in which a buyer sets out the proposed price and main terms before the detailed checking and the final contract.
GRO-11.Tax planning: With an accountant, the owner plans how to structure the sale so that as little of the price as legally possible goes to taxes.
GRO-11.Reduce dependence on the owner: The owner trains managers and writes procedures down so the business can run without him or her, which makes it worth more to a buyer.
GRO-11.Fix up the premises: Cleaning, repairing equipment and tidying the site help the business make a good first impression on buyers.
GRO-11.Notify employees and customers: At the right moment the owner tells staff, customers and suppliers about the change, to keep their trust and their business.
GRO-11.Offer seller financing: The seller agrees to be paid part of the price over time, which makes the purchase possible for more buyers.
GRO-11.Non-compete agreement: The seller promises not to open a rival business nearby for a set period, so the buyer keeps the customers that were paid for.
GRO-11.Prepare a selling memorandum: A written summary of the business, covering its history, finances, operations and prospects, that is given to serious buyers.
GRO-11.Transfer leases and licenses: The seller arranges for the lease, key contracts and any transferable licenses or permits to pass to the buyer.
GRO-11.Settle debts and liens: The seller pays off loans and clears any legal claims on the assets, so the buyer receives them free of old debts.
